A scan of the whole tree now reports **five** `.bak` files rather than the four recorded earlier, and the fifth is not stray junk: it is `.overlord/prime-agent-data/models.json.bak`, agent runtime state dated 2026, inside the `.overlord/` runtime this ledger forbids deleting wholesale. The four historical source backups are dated 2019, 2021, 2022, and 2024 and are untouched. The count of four refers to the source tree, and the discrepancy is recorded here so a later session does not read it as new litter.

**Not done, and not claimed.** This is a transport-free record codec. It does not open a socket, install keys, frame a live descriptor, apply inventory or window policy, check ownership or distance, decide how many units move, or reproduce the legacy handler. The three legacy defects that lose a horse, corrupt a Meley map iterator, and leak a stale quest NPC identifier all remain above this boundary. The persistent rewrite objective stays open; Section 142 has since been selected.


### Section 142 packing and `TItemPos` findings, verified directly

**Packing is confirmed for all three records, by measuring the pragma extent rather than assuming it.** `packet.h` contains exactly two packing directives: `#pragma pack(1)` at line **274** and `#pragma pack()` at line **3540**. The odd-count test at lines 1979, 1988, 1990, 1999, 2320, and 2326 all report packed, so both safebox structs and the Section 141 give-item struct lie inside a single packed region. This also re-confirms the Section 140 claim that the packing region is `packet.h:274..3540`.

**`TItemPos` is not a plain aggregate, and that is a fact a Rust boundary must not model away.** The server type is `typedef struct SItemPos { BYTE window_type; WORD cell; ... } TItemPos;` at `server/server/common/length.h:957-1059`, inside `#pragma pack(push, 1)` at `:956` and `#pragma pack(pop)` at `:1274`. Its two data members occupy exactly 3 bytes under that pragma, which is the number the codec depends on. But the type also carries **a user-provided default constructor**, two converting constructors, and roughly a dozen member functions, so it is not trivially default-constructible and is not an aggregate. Two consequences follow. First, the default constructor is not zero-filling: it sets `window_type = INVENTORY` and `cell = WORD_MAX`, so any local instance would begin life as the inventory sentinel `(1, 0xffff)` and not as zero. Second, and more useful for a wire boundary, `server/server/game` never runs that constructor on this path at all, because every handler reaches the record by C-style cast over received bytes, so the bytes on the wire are exactly what the sender wrote. This is the concrete reason the project rule against using a Rust packed struct as the compatibility representation keeps holding here, and it is a stronger reason than the usual alignment one: the legacy type has behaviour a compat struct would silently drop.

**A latent hazard worth recording, because it is the same shape as the confirmed client defect.** Because the default constructor produces `(INVENTORY, 0xffff)` deterministically and leaves any other member untouched, any code that declared a `TPacketCGSafeboxCheckout` as a local and then sent it would put a valid-looking inventory position on the wire together with an indeterminate safebox index. The client wrapper at `PythonNetworkStreamModule.cpp:1376-1377` does effectively this, and the fact that four of the five bytes are deterministic is exactly the mechanism described in Section 141.

**The position type's own validity rules reject safebox and mall outright, on both sides.** The server's `SItemPos::IsValidItemPosition()` at `length.h:1067` switches on `window_type` and returns `false` for both `SAFEBOX` and `MALL` before any cell bound is consulted. The client's `SItemPos::IsValidCell()` at `client/Client/UserInterface/GameType.h:438-461` has no `SAFEBOX` and no `MALL` case at all, so the same windows fall to its `default: return false`. The outcome matches, but by different routes, which is worth stating because it means no safebox path can rely on this member to validate the position it just received. Section 140 already established that the game server resolves item-position validity to `CHARACTER::IsValidItemPosition`; this is the disagreeing member, and it disagrees in a way that specifically forbids the two window types this section is about.

**A real naming divergence between the two trees for what appears to be the same feature.** The server guards the `ATTR67_ADD` case with `#if defined(__ATTR_6TH_7TH__)` at `length.h:1080`, while the client guards the same case with `#if defined(ENABLE_ATTR_6TH_7TH)` at `GameType.h:449`. The two macro names are not the same string, so a build could enable the feature on one side and not the other, after which the two `SItemPos` types would accept a different set of windows. Both also guard `SWITCHBOT` with `#ifdef ENABLE_SWITCHBOT`, which does match. This is recorded as a source fact, not as a claim that any shipped configuration disagrees, since no build of either tree was exercised here. It is another instance of the general rule already in this ledger: layout and feature flags are separate axes and neither one can be inferred from the other.

**Client-side parity of the position type is otherwise exact.** The client declares `typedef struct SItemPos` at `client/Client/UserInterface/GameType.h:422-507`, inside `#pragma pack (push, 1)` at `:418` and `#pragma pack(pop)` at `:508`, with the same `BYTE window_type; WORD cell;` members, the same default constructor producing `INVENTORY` and `WORD_MAX`, and the same two converting constructors. So both sides agree that the position is 3 packed bytes and that its default is `(1, 0xffff)`, which is what makes the Section 141 finding about deterministic bytes on a wrong arity apply identically here.


### Section 142 client audit, part 1: profile confirmed at 8 bytes on both sides, and a correction to my own audit brief

**The active profile is 8 bytes, and it cannot be turned off from inside this tree.** The client define at `LOCALE_INC.H:35` sits inside the `#ifdef PRODOMO_VERSION_4` block opened at `:23`, and `PRODOMO_VERSION_4` is itself defined unconditionally at `:7`, with no `#else` and no later `#undef`. A case-insensitive content sweep of the whole client tree, including binary and extension-less files, found exactly **one** `#define`, **zero** `#undef`, and no `.vcproj`, `.props`, or `.mak` override. The client width is therefore 8 bytes and the 5-byte alternative profile is unreachable in this tree. The audit independently re-derived the server side and reached the same conclusion, so the two trees agree.

**Correction to my own brief, recorded because the audit is the one that caught it.** When I dispatched the client audit I wrote that the builders assign "each of the nine (or five) bytes". **That is wrong: the record is 8 bytes, not 9.** The 8 bytes are `bHeader` at 0, `bSafePos`/`bMallPos` as a little-endian `DWORD` at 1..4, `ItemPos.window_type` at 5, and `ItemPos.cell` as a little-endian `WORD` at 6..7, with no padding. The 9-byte figure belongs to the sibling header 77, `HEADER_CG_SAFEBOX_ITEM_MOVE`, which reuses `TPacketCGItemMove` at client `Packet.h:529-535`. I carried the number over from the Section 141 give-item record, which is a different record that happens to also be 9 bytes. Two different records being the same size is exactly the kind of coincidence that a wrong claim hides inside, so the correction is worth recording rather than just fixing. The ledger's own Section 142 selection block already said 8 bytes and needed no change.

**The three client structs are byte-identical, and the rename is the only field-level difference.** After normalising the field name, the bodies of `command_safebox_checkout` (`Packet.h:789-798`), `command_safebox_checkin` (`:800-809`), and `command_mall_checkout` (`:811-820`) differ only in the struct tag and the typedef name. The field is `bSafePos` in the first two and `bMallPos` in the third. So the three headers 69, 70, and 71 carry **the same 8 bytes** and are distinguished only by byte 0. This strengthens the earlier point about not naming a codec after a container: the record is not "the safebox record" at all, it is the withdraw record with three identities.

**The three-client-struct / two-server-struct asymmetry is confirmed from both directions.** The client declares three types; the server declares two, and `packet_info.cpp:169` registers the mall header against `sizeof(TPacketCGSafeboxCheckout)`, so the server's mall field is also called `bSafePos`. A Rust boundary therefore has three wire identities, two legacy server type names, and three legacy client type names to describe, and the field name is the only thing that hints which identity was intended.

**A new and directly relevant fact: the feature flag changes the number of safebox pages, not only the record width.** `server/server/common/length.h:91-94` sets `SAFEBOX_MAX_PAGE_COUNT = 6` and `SAFEBOX_MAX_NUM = 45 * SAFEBOX_MAX_PAGE_COUNT` under the extended profile, and `server/server/common/tables.h:964-966` sets `SAFEBOX_MAX_NUM 135` for the non-extended one. So the flag changes the wire record from 8 bytes to 5 bytes **and** the valid index range from 6 pages to 3. This is the first evidence that the flag is a container-size switch rather than a mere alignment convenience, and it means the alternative profile is not only a different width but a different addressable space. It also sharpens what `bSafePos` can be: a page index, not a slot, since a safebox slot would be indexed by `ItemPos.cell` instead.


### Section 142 client audit, part 2: the three send builders, and a detected-but-still-sent out-of-range index

**All three builders write every byte, so the uninitialised-memory defect is NOT in the builder.** The three are `SendSafeBoxCheckinPacket` at `client/Client/UserInterface/PythonNetworkStreamPhaseGameItem.cpp:31-47`, `SendSafeBoxCheckoutPacket` at `:49-65`, and `SendMallCheckoutPacket` at `:169-185`, declared at `PythonNetworkStream.h:281-291`. Each declares a local `TPacketCGSafebox*`/`TPacketCGMallCheckout` and assigns the header byte, the slot `DWORD`, and the position, which is 8 assigned bytes in all three cases. The local is a plain aggregate with no user-provided constructor, so it is genuinely indeterminate before assignment, but because every field is written there is no indeterminate byte left in the record. This narrows Section 141's finding usefully: the leak is in the Python wrapper, not here, and I had been treating the wrapper and the builder as one site.

**The feature flag changes the C++ function signature, not only the struct.** Each builder has two declarations selected by the flag: `SendSafeBoxCheckinPacket(TItemPos, DWORD)` at `:32` versus `(TItemPos, BYTE)` at `:34`, `SendSafeBoxCheckoutPacket(DWORD, TItemPos)` at `:50` versus `(BYTE, TItemPos)` at `:52`, and `SendMallCheckoutPacket(DWORD, TItemPos)` at `:170` versus `(BYTE, TItemPos)` at `:172`. So `__EXTENDED_SAFEBOX__` changes the record width, the number of safebox pages, **and** the C++ parameter type of every builder. Any caller is therefore also profile-dependent, which is a third distinct axis for the same flag and further evidence that it is a feature switch rather than an alignment fix.

**Two API inconsistencies worth recording as source facts.** `SendSafeBoxCheckinPacket` takes the inventory position first and the safebox slot second, at `:32`, while the other two take the slot first and the position second, at `:50` and `:170`. And `SendSafeBoxCheckinPacket` writes its three fields in the order header, position, slot, at `:40-42`, so the slot word is written last and out of wire order, whereas the other two write header, slot, position. Neither affects the bytes on the wire, but both are easy to get wrong when reading the source and worth stating so a future implementation does not infer layout from assignment order.

**None of the three calls `__CanActMainInstance()`, and none logs a send failure.** All three are `if (!Send(...)) return false;` followed by `return SendSequence();`, with no `Tracef`, matching the pattern already recorded for the give-item builder. `SendSequence()` is the base no-op at `client/Client/EterLib/NetStream.cpp:856-859`, which is an unconditional `return true;`, and `CPythonNetworkStream` does not override it. So the only possible failure for any of these builders is the send-buffer capacity check.

**A confirmed defect: a bounds-checked bad index is logged and then sent anyway.** `__PlaySafeBoxItemDropSound` at `PythonNetworkStreamPhaseGameItem.cpp:710-719` and `__PlayMallItemDropSound` at `:721-730` do bounds-check the slot before playing a sound, calling `GetSlotItemID`/`GetSlotMallItemID` at `:714` and `:725` and logging "Strange slot index" from `client/Client/UserInterface/PythonSafeBox.cpp:55-66` and `:129-140`. The check therefore **detects and reports** an out-of-range safebox index, which means the legacy client genuinely does know the value is invalid. But the `return` at those sites exits only the sound helper: control returns to the builder at `:55` or `:175` and the record is transmitted regardless. So this is not an undetected malformed value but a detected one that is deliberately, or at least observably, still serialised. That is a sharper defect than a missing check, and it is the kind of thing a transport-free codec must neither fix nor reproduce: the codec preserves whatever 4-byte slot value the client chose.

**The inventory-position sound path validates nothing and logs nothing.** `__PlayInventoryItemDropSound` at `:690-697` calls `IAbstractPlayer::GetItemIndex`, implemented at `client/Client/UserInterface/PythonPlayer.cpp:647-653`, which returns 0 when `Cell.IsValidCell()` is false at `:649-650`. An invalid inventory position therefore produces a silent vnum 0 with no log at all, in contrast to the slot path that at least logs.

**`Send` only copies, and the client's packet-dump diagnostics are disabled.** `CNetworkStream::Send` at `client/Client/EterLib/NetStream.cpp:783-790` checks `size + 1` against remaining buffer space, copies, and returns; the TEA block is commented out at `:809-825`. The only trace it can emit is the `_PACKETDUMP` block at `:792-806`, and `_PACKETDUMP` is itself disabled at `NetStream.cpp:9`. So a rejected send produces no client-side diagnostic at all on this path, which is consistent with the discarded return value already recorded in Section 141.


### Section 142 client audit, parts 3 to 6, and a correction to my own Section 142 claim that my own tooling bug caused

**A bug in my own search produced a false claim in the Section 142 selection block, and the audit is what caught it.** I wrote that "neither 70 nor 71 collides across directions" and that this "distinguishes this pair from headers 11, 22, and 83". **That is wrong, and all three of 69, 70, and 71 do collide.** The cause was a malformed regular expression I used for the check. I searched with `HEADER_[CG]_\w+`, which requires exactly **one** letter between `HEADER_` and the next underscore, but every real name in this codebase has **two**, `CG` or `GC`. The pattern therefore matched **zero** of the 437 header declarations in `packet.h`; it could never have found anything, and its empty result was read as "no collision". I verified the defect directly: `re.findall(r"HEADER_[CG]_\w+", packet_h)` returns 0 matches while `re.findall(r"HEADER_(?:CG|GC)_\w+", packet_h)` returns 437. The lesson is the same shape as the earlier extension-glob mistake: **an empty result from a search is only evidence if the pattern was shown to match something.** I am recording the corrected pattern itself so the next session uses it and does not rediscover the same vacuous search.

**Corrected collision table, computed with the working pattern over both trees.**

| Value | Server client-to-game | Server game-to-client | Collision |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 69 | `HEADER_CG_MALL_CHECKOUT` | `HEADER_GC_ADD_FLY_TARGETING` | **yes** |
| 70 | `HEADER_CG_SAFEBOX_CHECKIN` | `HEADER_GC_CREATE_FLY` | **yes** |
| 71 | `HEADER_CG_SAFEBOX_CHECKOUT` | `HEADER_GC_FLY_TARGETING` | **yes** |
| 77 | `HEADER_CG_SAFEBOX_ITEM_MOVE` | `HEADER_GC_PARTY_INVITE` | **yes** |
| 83 | `HEADER_CG_ITEM_GIVE` | `HEADER_GC_PARTY_PARAMETER` | **yes** |
| 13 | `HEADER_CG_ITEM_MOVE` | `HEADER_GC_STUN` | **yes** |
| 11 | `HEADER_CG_ITEM_USE` | `HEADER_GC_CHARACTER_DELETE_WRONG_SOCIAL_ID` | **yes** |
| 15 | `HEADER_CG_ITEM_PICKUP` | `HEADER_GC_MAIN_CHARACTER_OLD` | **yes** |
| 22 | `HEADER_CG_ITEM_SELL` | `HEADER_GC_ITEM_USE` | **yes** |
| 52 | `HEADER_CG_USE_SKILL` | none | no |
| 60 | `HEADER_CG_ITEM_USE_TO_ITEM` | none | no |
| 105 | `HEADER_CG_HACK` | none | no |

The client's table agrees with the server's on every row, and the client additionally spells `HEADER_GC_PLAYER_DELETE_WRONG_SOCIAL_ID` where the server spells `HEADER_GC_CHARACTER_DELETE_WRONG_SOCIAL_ID` at value 11. The two earlier no-collision claims survive the corrected search, so Sections 137 and 140 stand: header 52 and header 60 really are unique in the client-to-game direction. The only claim this falsifies is the one I wrote minutes ago about 70 and 71.

**The client genuinely receives different records at 69, 70, and 71, so the hazard is concrete and not hypothetical.** The client registers the fly-targeting records inbound at `client/Client/UserInterface/PythonNetworkStream.cpp:100-102` and dispatches them at `client/Client/UserInterface/PythonNetworkStreamPhaseGame.cpp:444`, `:448`, and `:452`. So on the receive side the number 71 means a fly-targeting packet of some other width, while on the send side it means an 8-byte safebox withdrawal. The dead `_PACKETDUMP` name tables at `client/Client/EterLib/NetStream.cpp:567-569` and `:665-668` state the disagreement explicitly, though they are disabled at `NetStream.cpp:9`. Three colliding values at once is the worst case so far in the item family, and it makes the existing "never resolve a header through a table shared across directions" rule non-optional here.

**The safebox index is a flat cell index, not a page, which corrects my own speculation.** I had written that the flag's effect on `SAFEBOX_MAX_PAGE_COUNT` "sharpens what `bSafePos` can be: a page index, not a slot". **That is wrong.** `CPythonSafeBox::GetSlotItemID` at `client/Client/UserInterface/PythonSafeBox.cpp:55-63` indexes `m_ItemInstanceVector` directly with the value, and that vector is a flat one-entry-per-cell list resized at `PythonSafeBox.cpp:4-8` as `SAFEBOX_SLOT_X_COUNT * iSize` from a server-sent page count, not a two-level page-then-slot structure. The server consumes it as a cell index too, at `input_main.cpp:2310`, `:2385`, and `:2427`. So it is a **flat cell index into 5 columns times the page count**, and the client's own geometry at `PythonSafeBox.h:6-11` gives `SAFEBOX_SLOT_X_COUNT` 5, `SAFEBOX_SLOT_Y_COUNT` 9, and a derived `SAFEBOX_PAGE_SIZE` of 45, which is the source of the server's 45-per-page figure. The value is therefore a cell index, the page count only scales the valid range, and nothing on the wire encodes a page or a window for the container itself.

**The `TItemPos` is a destination cell for the two checkouts and a source cell for the checkin.** The server reads it as a source at `input_main.cpp:2287` with `ch->GetItem(p->ItemPos)`, and as a destination at `:2399` with `IsEmptyItemGrid(p->ItemPos, ...)`, with Dragon-Soul window branches at `:2409` and `:2433`. The same `window_type` byte serves both directions, so the record cannot be typed as "move to" or "move from" without also encoding a role that the wire does not carry.

**Correction to my Section 141 wrapper count, found in the third part of this audit.** I recorded that exactly three `default: break;` sites exist and that two of them reach a send with an uninitialised scalar. Both halves are right, but the conclusion I drew from them was too narrow, because **a third wrapper reaches a send with an indeterminate value without having any `default` label at all**. `netSendSafeboxCheckinPacket` at `client/Client/UserInterface/PythonNetworkStreamModule.cpp:1324-1353` switches on arity with only `case 2` at `:1331` and `case 3` at `:1338`, and simply falls out of the switch at `:1347` for arity 0, 1, 4, or more, then sends at `:1350`. I re-verified the whole module myself: of 13 `default:` labels, 11 return `Py_BuildException()` and exactly 2 are `break;`, at `:963` and `:1376`; the `:2333` private-shop filter is the third `break;` reached by the earlier scan but belongs to a different function shape. So the accurate statement is: **three wrappers can transmit an indeterminate 4-byte slot word** — give item at `:963`, safebox checkout at `:1376`, and safebox checkin at `:1347` by omission — while the mall wrapper at `:1425-1426` correctly returns before its send and is the one place in this record family where a bad arity does not reach the wire.

**The exposed bytes are exactly the 4-byte slot, and never the position.** Both safebox wrappers declare `int iSafeBoxPos;` with no initialiser at `:1327` and `:1357`, and that becomes wire bytes 1..4 in the active profile. Their `TItemPos InventoryPos;` at `:1326` and `:1358` is **not** indeterminate, because the `SItemPos` user-provided default constructor at `client/Client/UserInterface/GameType.h:426-430` runs and yields `window_type` 1 and `cell` 0xffff, with `INVENTORY` 1 and `WORD_MAX` 0xffff confirmed at `GameType.h:295-298` and `:419`. So a wrong arity sends 4 indeterminate bytes and 4 deterministic ones, not 7 indeterminate bytes. The client's own `NPOS` at `GameType.h:507` is `(RESERVED_WINDOW, WORD_MAX)`, window **0**, which is a different pair from what these wrappers produce, so it is not the sentinel in play here.

**A script-facing footgun worth recording: the two safebox wrappers take the same two arguments in opposite order.** The 2-argument checkin form is `(inventory cell, safebox slot)` at `:1333` and `:1335`, while the 2-argument checkout form is `(safebox slot, inventory cell)` at `:1363` and `:1365`. The 3-argument forms differ too, being `(window, cell, slot)` at `:1339-1343` and `(slot, window, cell)` at `:1369-1373`. The C++ signatures differ the same way, with checkin taking `(TItemPos, DWORD)` and the other two taking `(DWORD, TItemPos)` at `client/Client/UserInterface/PythonNetworkStream.h:282-285`. A script that calls checkin and checkout with the same argument list therefore transposes the slot and the cell, and the wire carries a plausible-looking 8-byte record either way. This is a source fact about the legacy scripting API, not something a wire codec may normalise.

**A profile detail that makes the flag observable by design.** `client/Client/UserInterface/PythonApplicationModule.cpp:1804-1808` exports `__EXTENDED_SAFEBOX__` to the interpreter as a module integer constant, `true` in this tree. It adds no bytes and does not alter the record, but it shows the profile is meant to be visible to scripts, and since the gameplay scripts are absent from this worktree nothing here consumes it.

**Script-side behaviour remains undetermined, and the audit said so rather than guessing.** A case-insensitive sweep finds exactly one `.py` file under the whole client tree, `client/Client/UserInterface/Version.py`, which is a Perforce version-stamp generator that shells out to `p4 changes` and rewrites `Version.h`; there are no `.pyc` or `.pyo` files and no `ui*` directory. So which script calls these three names, with which arity, and under what conditions cannot be determined from this tree. The three names are registered as `METH_VARARGS` at `PythonNetworkStreamModule.cpp:2624`, `:2625`, and `:2629`, which constrains nothing about arity.


### Section 142 server audit: profile is compile-time, and the two handlers diverge in ways that must stay out of the codec

**The 8-byte profile is a compile-time constant, not a runtime feature profile, which is a cleaner answer than the DB boot path gives.** `server/server/common/prodomodefines.h:61` is the only `#define __EXTENDED_SAFEBOX__` in the server tree, it is not wrapped in any `#if`, and a sweep of all 14,487 files under `server/` across every extension found **11** occurrences total: that one define plus ten `#if` uses at `length.h:91`, `tables.h:964`, `packet.h:1449`, `:1982`, `:1993`, `safebox.h:19`, `:24`, `safebox.cpp:164`, `:178`, and `input_db.cpp:1146`, with **zero** `#undef` and zero build-system mentions. Producing the 5-byte shape would require editing that one source line, which is a source change and not a configuration. So the 5-byte alternative is dead in this tree, and unlike the DB boot feature profile this one cannot be selected at run time. The include chain was also verified rather than assumed: `length.h:4` and `game/stdafx.h:16` both include `prodomodefines.h`, `packet.h:3` includes `stdafx.h`, and `input_main.cpp:51` includes it directly.

**The legacy server enforces the record length before the handler ever sees the bytes, so there is no out-of-bounds read here.** `server/server/game/input.cpp:83` looks the size up through `CPacketInfo::Get` (`packet_info.cpp:33-45`), `:92-93` refuses to continue while fewer than that many bytes are buffered, and `:100` only then calls `Analyze`. So the bare cast at `input_main.cpp:2370` is always in bounds, and `iExtraLen` stays 0 for these headers because the case bodies at `:3804-3815` only call a handler and break, with `iExtraLen` initialised to 0 at `:3654`. This is worth contrasting with the DB peer path already recorded in this ledger, where length is not trusted; here the fixed-size table makes the read safe, and a Rust frame adapter should require exactly **7** payload bytes.

**The three headers are not three roles of one operation: only header 70 moves an item in.** `HEADER_CG_SAFEBOX_CHECKIN` at `input_main.cpp:3804-3806` calls `SafeboxCheckin`, which reads the item out of the character with `ch->GetItem(p->ItemPos)` at `:2287` and puts it **into** the container with `pkSafebox->Add(p->bSafePos, pkItem)` at `:2361`. The other two remove an item **out of** a container via `pkSafebox->Remove(p->bSafePos)` at `:2427` and `:2445`. So `TPacketCGSafeboxCheckin` is a distinct type with an identical layout but the **opposite** direction, and calling all three "the same record" would be wrong in the only sense that matters semantically. The mall header reaches `ch->GetMall()` at `:2378` and the safebox header `ch->GetSafebox()` at `:2380`.

**The mall branch is a strict superset of the safebox branch's mutations, with no skipped validation.** `bMall` occurs at exactly four lines, `:2368`, `:2377`, `:2404`, and `:2456`. The container differs, the log label differs, and the mall branch additionally runs `DSManager::DragonSoulItemInitialize(pkItem)` at `:2406`. Every validation from `:2372` through `:2443` runs identically on both branches: `CanHandleItem()` at `:2372`, the null-container check at `:2382`, the null-item check at `:2387`, the custom-inventory category check at `:2390-2397`, `IsEmptyItemGrid` at `:2399`, and the Dragon-Soul and belt window checks at `:2409`, `:2416`, `:2433`, and `:2439`. So the mall path is not a laxer variant; it does strictly more.

**A confirmed ordering defect: the mall branch mutates the item before validating the transfer.** `DragonSoulItemInitialize` at `server/server/game/DragonSoul.cpp:383-392` calls `PutAttributes(pItem)` at `:387` and rewrites socket 0 with `pItem->SetSocket(ITEM_SOCKET_REMAIN_SEC, time)` at `:390`. The call at `input_main.cpp:2406` happens **before** the destination-window check at `:2409-2413` and before the cell check at `:2416`. A client that sends header 69 with a Dragon-Soul item and a non-Dragon-Soul window therefore has the item's attributes and its remaining-seconds socket rewritten and then gets nothing transferred at all. Its `bool` result is discarded as well. The safebox branch cannot do this.

**A confirmed asymmetry: the protected-inventory gate exists on the mall load path and is absent on the safebox load path.** `CHARACTER::LoadMall` at `server/server/game/char.cpp:7210-7216` has an `IsSecured()` check under `__ENABLE_INVENTORY_PROTECTED_SYSTEM__`, while `CHARACTER::LoadSafebox` at `char.cpp:7102-7159` goes straight from its signature to `bool bLoaded = false;` at `:7104`. The feature is live, since the macro is defined at `prodomodefines.h:169`, so this is an active divergence and not a compiled-out branch.

**Neither wire handler consults the protected state at all, which is a confirmed defect against the house pattern.** A full-tree grep finds **zero** `IsSecured()` occurrences in `input_main.cpp`, while the sibling item paths enforce it at `char_item.cpp:1425`, `:1600`, `:7236`, `:7430`, `:7490`, `:7717`, `:10184`, `:10213`, `char.cpp:7055`, `:11894`, `:11911`, `shop_manager.cpp:412`, `exchange.cpp:106`, and others. The two safebox handlers, at `:2276-2366` and `:2368-2460`, have none in their 91 and 93 lines.

**A confirmed defect with real consequences: an equipped item can be checked into the safebox.** `SafeboxCheckin` reads its source with no window restriction at `input_main.cpp:2287`, and `CHARACTER::GetItem` accepts the `EQUIPMENT` window at `char_item.cpp:262-269`, with the whole wear range valid because `INVENTORY_MAX_NUM` is 180 at `length.h:25` and `WEAR_MAX_NUM` is 64 at `length.h:89`. The only `IsEquipped()` reference in the handler, at `input_main.cpp:2334-2348`, is inside `ENABLE_WEAPON_COSTUME_SYSTEM` and only handles the costume weapon, so it never rejects a general equipped item. The unequip then happens as a side effect of `CItem::RemoveFromCharacter` at `item.cpp:369-377`, which calls `Unequip()`, sets `RESERVED_WINDOW`, and saves, triggered from `input_main.cpp:2358`. Nothing gates this and it is normal-client reachable.

**Several house checks that sibling handlers apply are absent here, listed so a future adapter does not assume them.** Against the nearest analogue, `CHARACTER::DestroyItem` at `char_item.cpp:7407-7441`, the safebox checkin is missing `IsExchanging()` at `:7420`, `GetCount() <= 0` at `:7426`, and `IsSecured()` at `:7430`; and both handlers are missing `GetShopOwner()` and `GetExchange()`, which are present only at the one-time load gate in `input_db.cpp:1138`. `isLocked()` **is** present in the checkin at `input_main.cpp:2328-2332` and is correctly absent from the checkout, since a checkout moves an item toward the player rather than away. Notably `IsExchanging()` does exist inside the shared container helper at `safebox.cpp:194-195`, so the concept is available in the very same file and is simply omitted from both wire handlers. `CanHandleItem()` at `char_item.cpp:213-247` blocks `GetMyShop()` at `:219` and the refine, cube, warp, sash, aura, and changelog states at `:222-243`, but blocks neither `GetShopOwner()` nor `GetExchange()`.

**A confirmed discard-the-result defect in both handlers, with an item-orphaning failure mode.** The checkin detaches the item at `input_main.cpp:2358` before adding it to the container at `:2361`, and `CSafebox::Add` can return `false` at `safebox.cpp:61` after the pre-check at `input_main.cpp:2310` has already passed; the `bool` is dropped. The checkout removes from the container at `:2427` before `pkItem->AddToCharacter(ch, DestPos)` at `:2428` and again at `:2445-2446`, and `CItem::AddToCharacter` returns `false` on a cell overflow at `item.cpp:452` and `:461`, with both `bool` results dropped. In the checkin case the window of failure is provably narrow, because the pre-check at `:2310` and `IsValidPosition` apply the same bound, so this is recorded as a discard-the-result defect with a latent orphaning mode rather than as a proven reachable loss. One incidental oddity worth keeping: the overflow guard at `item.cpp:449` tests `m_wCell`, the item's **current** cell, not the destination `pos` parameter.


### Section 142 server audit, continued: reachability, container geometry, and the dead 5-byte declaration already in the tree

**The three registrations are unconditional in the source, and observer mode is blocked only indirectly.** Neither the `Set(...)` calls at `packet_info.cpp:153`, `:154`, and `:169` nor the three `case` labels at `input_main.cpp:3804`, `:3807`, and `:3813` sit inside any `#ifdef`, unlike the DB boot profile this ledger has modelled before. The neighbouring `case` bodies at `:3689-3692` and `:3693-3698` carry an explicit `if (!ch->IsObserverMode())` gate; the three safebox cases carry none. Observer mode is still blocked, but only because `CanHandleItem()` is the first statement of both handlers at `:2372` and `:2283` and it tests `m_bIsObserver` at `char_item.cpp:213-217`. The real gate for all three headers is therefore runtime container state, not a build flag or a dispatch predicate.

**A confirmed reachability asymmetry: a dead character can still use the mall header.** `CInputMain::Analyze` serves both `PHASE_GAME` and `PHASE_DEAD`, because `desc.cpp:526-532` binds `m_pInputProcessor = &m_inputMain` for both. The `CInputDead` processor at `desc.h:197` is dead code: a whole-tree grep for `m_inputDead` returns exactly one hit, the declaration itself, and it is never assigned. On death `CHARACTER::Dead` calls `CloseSafebox()` at `char_battle.cpp:1648`, nulling `m_pkSafebox` at `char.cpp:7189-7191`, so headers 70 and 71 return immediately at the `!pkSafebox` guards at `input_main.cpp:2289` and `:2382`. `CloseMall()` is **not** in `CHARACTER::Dead`; it appears only at `char.cpp:1806` inside `Disconnect` and at `cmd_general.cpp:1055`. So a dead character that still has the mall open reaches `SafeboxCheckout(ch, c_pData, true)` with no `IsDead()` check anywhere in the handler. This is normal-client reachable with no observer or build gate.

**Neither container is reachable from a bare packet.** The mall is created only in `CHARACTER::LoadMall` at `char.cpp:7224`, which is called only from `CInputDB::MallLoad` at `input_db.cpp:1216`, and the only requester of `HEADER_GD_MALL_LOAD` is the GM command at `cmd_general.cpp:1047`. So header 69 is always parsed but does nothing until a GM has opened the mall. The safebox is created at `char.cpp:7114` from `CInputDB::SafeboxLoad` at `input_db.cpp:1119-1152`, which needs a client safebox-load request with a password and applies its own state gate at `input_db.cpp:1138`. Once open, headers 70 and 71 are unconditionally reachable, and the safebox is closed only by `cmd_general.cpp:978`, by `Disconnect` at `char.cpp:1804`, or by death. It is not closed by opening a shop or an exchange, and neither handler re-checks those.

**The `u32` field is a flat cell index, and the exact accepted ranges are now computed.** `CSafebox` always builds `CGrid(5, m_iSize)` at `safebox.cpp:18`, so the index space is five columns by `m_iSize` rows. The safebox sets `m_iSize = bSize * SAFEBOX_PAGE_SIZE` at `input_db.cpp:1151` with `SAFEBOX_PAGE_SIZE = 9` at `char.h:81`, and `bSize` is `1` by default at `input_db.cpp:1135` or `SAFEBOX_MAX_PAGE_COUNT = 6` at `length.h:92`, giving `m_iSize` of 9 or 54 and therefore a valid index of `[0, 45)` or `[0, 270)`. The mall is a literal `3 * SAFEBOX_PAGE_SIZE` = 27 at `char.cpp:7224`, so its index is `[0, 135)`. The backing array `LPITEM m_pkItems[SAFEBOX_MAX_NUM]` at `safebox.h:41` is sized `45 * SAFEBOX_MAX_PAGE_COUNT` = 270 at `length.h:93`, exactly the largest grid. The client splits the returned position back apart using only the `.cell` half at `PythonNetworkStreamPhaseGameItem.cpp:108` and `:121`, which independently confirms the cell reading and shows the client treats the window byte as implied by the window it is drawing.

**Every out-of-range value fails closed; the legacy server never clamps, wraps, or takes a modulo.** `CSafebox::Get` returns `NULL` for an index at or beyond the grid size at `safebox.cpp:95-96`; `CSafebox::IsValidPosition` returns false at `:251-260`; and `CGrid::IsEmpty` at `grid.cpp:86-96` returns false for a negative position, for a row overflow, and for a width that would wrap. The single place the item array is indexed without its own bound is `CSafebox::Add` at `safebox.cpp:70`, reachable only through the DB peer: `CInputDB::SafeboxChangeSize` at `input_db.cpp:1154-1165` takes an unbounded `BYTE` from the peer and can rebuild the grid up to `5*255 = 1275` cells, while the array holds 270. That is a DB-peer precondition, not a game-client one, and it belongs with the DB peer hardening boundary already recorded in this ledger. The same caution applies to `CGrid::Get` at `grid.cpp:68-82`, which bounds-checks only `iPos` and not `iStart`, so a valid last-row cell plus a multi-cell item can write past the grid; `CGrid::Put` and `CGrid::IsEmpty` are safe.

**The record has no count field at all, and the transfer is always the whole item.** `CSafebox::Remove` at `safebox.cpp:101-125` never calls `SetCount`, and `CSafebox::Add` at `:56-91` never splits a stack. The only count machinery on this container belongs to the sibling move header 77 at `safebox.cpp:211-220`. This is a useful contrast with Section 141, whose dead `byItemCount` byte at least exists on the wire.

**A confirmed narrowing defect at the caller layer.** `input_main.cpp:2360` passes `p->ItemPos.cell`, a `WORD` from `length.h:960`, to `SyncQuickslot`'s `BYTE bOldPos` parameter at `char.h:1035`. For any cell at or above 256 the quickslot that gets deleted is not the one the client named. The default inventory tops out at 180 so it does not fire there, but the custom-inventory layout reaches roughly 1370, so the belt and custom ranges are affected. It is a caller-layer defect and is deliberately not reproduced in the codec.

**The mall path can write a broken Dragon-Soul item into a player's inventory.** `DragonSoulItemInitialize` returns `bool` and returns false at `DragonSoul.cpp:386`, and `PutAttributes` itself returns false at `:308`, `:319`, `:325`, and `:331`; none of those is consulted at `input_main.cpp:2406`. A failed initialisation therefore still yields a Dragon-Soul item with uninitialised attributes.

**An in-tree declaration that is wrong for the active profile already exists, in a file that is not compiled.** `/workspace/protocol/src/cg.rs:458-474` declares `TPacketCGSafeboxCheckout` and `TPacketCGSafeboxCheckin` with `b_safe_pos: u8`, which is the 5-byte dead shape, and embeds a `TItemPos` at `lib.rs:545-553` that is neither `#[repr(C)]` nor `#[repr(packed)]`. That file is 19,979 bytes and is **not** registered in `lib.rs`, which is why this ledger records that there is no live `protocol::cg` module, so it cannot be compiled and cannot affect any gate. The live inventory is already correct and records `base_size: 8` for headers 71, 70, and 69 at `protocol/src/cg_inventory.rs:757-763`, `:764-770`, and `:869-875`. This file is recorded as a cleanup candidate and was deliberately left in place in this slice; the new codec does not reuse it, because `AGENTS.md` requires a field-by-field codec rather than a `#[repr(C)]` mirror.


### Section 142 implementation: the second record in this series to store a header, and the first with three

**The record.** `protocol/src/cg_safebox.rs` is the new transport-free codec. It models all three wire identities at once and is the first fixed client record in this series whose width is not a constant of the legacy source. Active layout, eight bytes, no padding:

```text
offset 0      header        0x45, 0x46, or 0x47
offset 1..5   container_pos explicit little-endian u32
offset 5      window_type   opaque byte
offset 6..8   cell          explicit little-endian u16
```

**Why this record stores a header, and a correction to how that claim was first written.** The standing rule in this series is to omit a header field when a record has exactly one encodable value, because a second copy in memory could only create a state the encoder cannot emit. This record breaks that rule because the header is a genuine wire field with three legal values, all three must round-trip, and the three carry different transfer directions, so it is stored as a closed `SafeBoxKind` enum. **An earlier draft of this section claimed this was the first record in the series to store a header, and that was wrong.** `protocol/src/cg_handshake.rs` already defines `CgInboundHandshake` with a stored `header: CgHandshakeHeader`, because the inbound handshake record accepts two header values, `0xff` and `0xfc`, and must not normalise one to the other. So the correct statement is that this is the **second** record in the series to store a header deliberately, and the first with **three** legal values. The error was found by sweeping the whole protocol crate for structs with a stored `header` or `b_header` field after the review had already gone out; the sweep also found `LegacyCgPacket` in `cg_inventory.rs` and `ClientFrame` in `cg_wire.rs`, which are registry and transport types rather than record codecs and are not precedents. The wrong sentence is left here beside its correction rather than deleted. The enum is closed: only `MallCheckout` (0x45), `SafeboxCheckin` (0x46), and `SafeboxCheckout` (0x47) can be constructed, and `from_header` returns `None` for every other byte, so no state exists that the encoder cannot emit. This is the one place in the series where the no-stored-header rule is deliberately not applied, and the reason is recorded in the module docs.

**The direction distinction is a source fact, exposed but not applied.** `SafeBoxKind::is_deposit()` returns true only for `SafeboxCheckin`, because only that identity reaches `CInputMain::SafeboxCheckin`, which calls `pkSafebox->Add(p->bSafePos, pkItem)` at `input_main.cpp:2361`. The other two reach `CInputMain::SafeboxCheckout`, which calls `pkSafebox->Remove(p->bSafePos)` at `:2427` and `:2445`. The same `window_type` byte is a source cell for header 70 and a destination cell for headers 69 and 71, so the record cannot be typed as move-to or move-from without inventing a role the wire does not carry; the codec leaves it as one `CgItemPos` and documents the asymmetry instead.

**The feature profile is a compile-time constant, and only the 8-byte shape is implemented.** `prodomodefines.h:61` and client `LOCALE_INC.H:35` are the only two definitions, neither tree has an `#undef` or a build override, and there are ten `#if` uses. Producing the 5-byte shape would require editing the `#define`, which is a source change, so the module documents `CG_SAFEBOX_LEGACY_WIRE_SIZE = 5` as a constant and provides no function that produces or accepts that shape. This is deliberately different from the DB boot feature profile already recorded in this ledger, which is selected at run time; conflating the two would have been an error.

**Both fields stay opaque and unvalidated.** The `u32` is preserved verbatim with no clamp, wrap, or capacity check, because the legacy container rejects an out-of-range index by returning `NULL` or `false` rather than altering it, and because the client wrappers can put an uninitialised `int` in those four bytes. `window_type` is preserved verbatim with no allowlist, because the legacy server never applies one; it is constrained only indirectly, by `CHARACTER::IsValidItemPosition` at `char_item.cpp:10010-10045` and `CHARACTER::IsEmptyItemGrid` at `:737-1036`, both of which fail closed. The struct-level `SItemPos::IsValidItemPosition` returns `false` for `SAFEBOX` and `MALL` at `length.h:985-987`, so borrowing that predicate would have rejected every legitimate use of this record, and the module docs say so explicitly.

**Decoder discipline is the same invariant as every other record in the series.** Both `decode` and `decode_frame` check the exact total length of eight bytes before reading the header, and the header before reading any field. A short framed payload is `Truncated`, a long one is `LengthMismatch`, and a length error takes precedence over `InvalidHeader`. The framed path is tested by building a frame with a **correct** seven-byte payload and a wrong header, because pairing a wrong header with a wrong length would only ever exercise the length branch.

**Reuse, not duplication.** The module reuses the shared `CgItemPos` from `cg_item_move` and re-exports `CG_ITEM_POS_SIZE`, so the item codecs cannot drift. It adds no second framer, no packed `#[repr(C)]` compatibility struct, and no `unsafe`, and it required **no** change to `cg_inventory.rs` or `cg_wire.rs`: the active inventory already resolved all three headers to a fixed eight-byte frame. Exactly one line was added to `lib.rs`.

**Verification.** Twelve tests, taking the protocol crate from 304 to 316 unit tests. They cover the golden bytes of all three identities and the fact that they differ only in byte 0, the shared position offset, `u32` and window and cell boundary round-trips including `u32::MAX`, the `is_deposit` direction fact, raw and framed length-before-header precedence, exhaustive header validation over all 256 byte values at the correct length, byte-at-a-time fragmented streaming with tail retention, agreement between bulk and fragmented feeds, and error display.

**Seven mutations were applied and all seven were caught**, with the source restored byte-for-byte after each and the baseline SHA-256 re-checked: deleting the raw header check, deleting the framed header check, inverting the framed header/length order, inverting the raw header/length order, relaxing the framed length check from exact to minimum, writing `container_pos` big-endian, and swapping the `is_deposit` answer. A first attempt at the framed inversion survived, but inspection showed the mutation was malformed and still checked length first; the corrected mutation was caught, and the malformed attempt is recorded here rather than quietly dropped.

**All seven locked gates pass**: `cargo build`, `cargo test --workspace --all-targets`, `cargo clippy -- -D warnings`, `cargo fmt --check`, `RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc`, `cargo test --doc`, all with `--locked --offline`. The receipt is 996 tests across 27 test binaries plus 6 workspace doc-tests, 1002 in total, with zero failures.

**Corrections recorded from this slice rather than smoothed over.** A `HEADER_[CG]_\w+` search pattern that matched zero of the 437 header declarations in `packet.h` and produced a false "no cross-direction collision" result for headers 70 and 71; a claim that this record is nine bytes when it is eight; a claim that the index is a page number when it is a flat cell index; and a count of two indeterminate-slot wrappers when it is three. The corrected cross-direction table is now 11, 13, 15, 22, 69, 70, 71, 77, and 83 colliding, and 52 and 60 free.


### Section 143 selected: header 77, the safebox and mall in-container item move

**Header 77 is not a new record shape at all; it is the Section 138 item-move record under a second header value.** `server/server/game/packet_info.cpp:157` registers it as `Set(HEADER_CG_SAFEBOX_ITEM_MOVE, sizeof(TPacketCGItemMove), "SafeboxItemMove")`, so the C++ size table reuses the very same `TPacketCGItemMove` type that header 13 uses. `server/server/game/packet.h:61` sets the value to 77, and the client agrees independently at `client/Client/UserInterface/Packet.h:58`. This is the mirror image of Section 142: there, three headers shared two structs; here, one header shares a struct with another header and does something completely different with it.

**The handler is twelve lines and ignores both window bytes.** `CInputMain::SafeboxItemMove` at `server/server/game/input_main.cpp:2462-2473` is the whole of it:

```text
2464    struct command_item_move * pinfo = (struct command_item_move *) data;
2466    if (!ch->CanHandleItem())
2467        return;
2469    if (!ch->GetSafebox())
2470        return;
2472    ch->GetSafebox()->MoveItem(pinfo->Cell.cell, pinfo->CellTo.cell, pinfo->count);
```

It is dispatched at `input_main.cpp:3810-3812`. The cast is a bare C-style cast on data the length gate already vouched for, matching the pattern in the Section 142 handlers. The decisive observation is that the call site reads only `Cell.cell` and `CellTo.cell`; the two `window_type` bytes are never read on this path at all. That is a materially different fact from a window byte that is read and validated, and it means the shared position type cannot be treated as a role-bearing pair here. There is no safebox-specific struct anywhere in the legacy source for this header, which is itself worth recording, because the naming in `packet_info.cpp` and the handler name both suggest one exists.

**This makes Section 143 a design question rather than a layout question, and the same one Section 142 posed.** `CgItemMove` in `protocol/src/cg_item_move.rs` deliberately stores no header and always encodes 13, because Section 138 established that header 13 was the only encodable value. Header 77 needs the same nine bytes with a different byte 0. So the slice is not "write a new codec" but "decide how a second legal header value attaches to an existing codec that currently has none", and the answer must not break the Section 138 contract that its 29 tests and the ledger receipt both rely on. The candidate options are a separate record type that shares the position pair, or a header-carrying identity added to the existing type; the second would change a receipted module and needs a deliberate argument for why that is better than duplicating a nine-byte codec.

**Collision already recorded.** Header 77 collides with `HEADER_GC_PARTY_INVITE`, which is on the already-receipted collision table above. The full sweep of Section 143, including the client builder, the Python wrapper and its argument order, the `CSafebox::MoveItem` validation and grid reachability, the count semantics, and the client inbound layout of the colliding game-to-client record, is running as a separate read-only audit. Those results are not yet in, and nothing in this section should be treated as final until they are.


### Section 142 independent review: PASS, and every finding fixed

The independent read-only review returned **PASS** with no BLOCKER and no MAJOR. It re-verified the wire size, the unreachable 5-byte profile, the three header values, all three cross-direction collisions, the `is_deposit` direction fact, the absence of clamping, the decoder precedence order, the closed enum, the reuse of `CgItemPos`, and the fact that `cg_wire.rs` needed no change and `cg_inventory.rs` already carried the correct `base_size: 8` at `:761`, `:768`, and `:873`. It also **withdrew its own earlier clippy BLOCKER**, which it had measured against a scratch copy taken before those fixes landed, and re-measured all four gates clean on a fresh copy. That withdrawal is the reviewer's and is recorded as such; the substance is that the strict-clippy gate passes.

**Six findings were raised and all six are fixed. Four were real errors in my documentation.**

1. **The `SyncQuickslot` narrowing named the wrong field, and it was mine.** `input_main.cpp:2360` is `ch->SyncQuickslot(QUICKSLOT_TYPE_ITEM, p->ItemPos.cell, 255)`, so the `WORD` narrowed to the `BYTE bOldPos` parameter of `char.h:1035` is `ItemPos.cell` at `length.h:960`, **not** `bSafePos`. Under the active profile `bSafePos` is a `DWORD` at `packet.h:1982-1983` and never reaches that call at all. My consequence sentence was right and my subject was wrong. Fixed.
2. **The "thirteenth of them" ordinal was false and self-contradictory**, since the same paragraph said twelve. The reviewer enumerated every `TPacketCG*` struct in `packet.h` programmatically: exactly **twelve** embed a packed `TItemPos`, and the Section 141 list already contains both safebox records, so these are the **tenth and eleventh of twelve** and there is no thirteenth. The true ordinal is that this is the **fifth** Rust codec to reuse the shared `CgItemPos`, after item-move, item-use, item-use-to-item, and item-give. Fixed.
3. **"the first whose width is not a constant of the source" was also wrong.** `TPacketCGExchange` at `packet.h:724-735` comes earlier in declaration order and is likewise profile-dependent, because `ENABLE_REMOVE_LIMIT_GOLD` at `prodomodefines.h:157` swaps a `DWORD` for an `unsigned long long`, changing the packed width from 10 to 14. Reworded to "the first of the twelve whose packed width is profile-dependent rather than fixed".
4. **"declares two packed record types" was true of the server but not of the client.** The client declares three, adding a separate `TPacketCGMallCheckout` whose container field is named `bMallPos` at `client/Client/UserInterface/Packet.h:811-820`. All three client types are 8 bytes packed and the wire is unaffected, but the sentence cited both trees while counting only the server's. Fixed.
5. **`CgSafeBoxItem::header()` had no coverage and a mutation proved it.** The reviewer made the accessor always return the check-in header and **all twelve tests stayed green**, because `encode_into` and `to_frame` were calling `self.kind.header()` directly and bypassing it. Fixed properly rather than by deleting the accessor: both encoders now call `self.header()`, so there is one point of truth, and two tests were added, one asserting the accessor agrees with the stored kind and the encoded byte 0, and one asserting that `window_type` stays opaque by round-tripping **all 256** window bytes in both the raw and the framed path, including the two windows the struct-level legacy predicate rejects.
6. **The framed length used `payload.len() + 1` rather than the house saturating add.** Aligned to `saturating_add(1)`, which is what `cg_item_move::CgItemMove::decode_frame` uses. The reviewer's companion observation that `SafeBoxKind::from_header` matches bare `0x45`/`0x46`/`0x47` literals because a `const` cannot be a match pattern was accepted as correct and is pinned by `active_inventory_agrees_on_all_three_headers`.

**Two further citations were correct but loose, and both are now precise.** The line `safebox.cpp:194-195` is the `IsExchanging` check, not an `IsSecured` one, and `safebox.cpp` contains no `IsSecured` at all; the text now names `IsExchanging` explicitly so it is not read as a source for the missing protected-state gate. And `:1355` is the signature of `netSendSafeboxCheckoutPacket`, not an argument read; the actual reads are the checkin cell at `:1333` and slot at `:1335` versus the checkout slot at `:1363` and cell at `:1365`.

**Mutation strength after the fixes: seventeen mutations applied, seventeen caught.** In addition to the seven already recorded, the reviewer's ten were re-run and reproduced: the previously **surviving** accessor mutation is now caught by the new test, and three further mutations were added to pin the opaqueness claims, namely a `window_type` allowlist in the raw decoder, a `window_type` allowlist in the framed decoder, and clamping `container_pos` to the largest legal safebox index of 269. All three are caught, which is what makes the two opacity claims testable rather than merely asserted. The source was restored byte-for-byte after every mutation.

**One incidental fact the review surfaced, recorded for the cleanup decision.** `protocol/src/cg.rs` is unregistered and never compiled, but `tools/packet_compare/src/main.rs:2` does `use protocol::cg::*`. The `tools` directory is outside the locked workspace, so that crate is never built either, which is why the stale `#[repr(C)]` safebox declarations in `cg.rs` have never produced a compile error. This explains how a wrong-width declaration survived in the tree and is part of the cleanup case.

**The receipt after the fixes is 998 tests across 27 test binaries plus 6 workspace doc-tests, 1004 in total, with all seven locked gates green.**

### The dead `cg.rs` and the `packet_compare` tool: three barriers, now decided for a cleanup slice

The `use protocol::cg::*` line is therefore not even reachable. There are **three independent barriers**, and `cg.rs` is the third and last, not the cause:

1. **Not a workspace member.** `tools/packet_compare/Cargo.toml` uses `[lints] workspace = true` and `bytes = { workspace = true }`, so it *requires* workspace membership, but the root `members` list of eight crates omits it and `exclude` never mentions it. Cargo hard-stops at manifest resolution with "current package believes it's in a workspace when it's not". Fatal before any Rust is compiled.
2. **`clap` cannot resolve.** The root `Cargo.lock` has 267 packages and **no** `clap` entry, and there is no `clap-*` in the offline registry cache, so the dependency fails to resolve offline and locked alike. Fatal and entirely independent of any Rust code.
3. **`use protocol::cg::*` at `tools/packet_compare/src/main.rs:2`.** Only ever reached if the first two were fixed.

**Has that tool ever built? No, and this is conclusive rather than suggestive.** A crate that had ever been resolved as a workspace member would appear in the root lock, and the lock contains no `packet_compare` entry and no `clap` entry. There is also no `tools/packet_compare/Cargo.lock`, and no `.d` artifact anywhere in the tree references it. The history does run out here: `tools/` is untracked and `Cargo.lock` is explicitly not tracked, so there is no committed history to consult. The mtimes are consistent with one authoring session, `cg.rs` at 2026-03-16 20:11, `packet_compare/Cargo.toml` at 19:59, and `main.rs` at 20:14, with the curated workspace manifest and lock both dated 2026-09-23. That ordering is suggestive rather than proof and is not treated as proof here, but the lockfile content is conclusive for the current state.

**Consequence for the cleanup decision, which is now decidable rather than open.** Deleting the stale `cg.rs` is the right call, and "register and fix" is the more expensive option that buys nothing, because the tool cannot build either way: it would need membership added, `clap` vendored or fetched, and its imports rewritten regardless. The decisive point is that `cg.rs` is a **916-line, 91-struct** monolith dated 2026-03-16 that the sixteen real `cg_*.rs` modules, all dated 2026-09-23 or later, have superseded one by one; the reviewer confirmed it is absent from `lib.rs`'s twenty-three modules, so nothing in the workspace compiles it today. It is also actively misleading, because its safebox record is the dead 5-byte profile and under `#[repr(C)]` it measures **6 bytes**, wrong for the active 8-byte build. That is precisely the stale oracle a future reader would trust. Deleting it also leaves no dangling import, since that line is its only reference.

**The deletion is deliberately NOT performed inside the Section 142 slice.** The evidence gathered here is recorded so the decision is made once, on its merits, in a dedicated cleanup slice with its own exact file list, its own measurement, and its own before-and-after receipt. A codec slice must not quietly delete neighbouring files. The one thing recorded here as a constraint on that future slice is that `tools/packet_compare/src/main.rs:2` will still name the module, so the slice must either delete the tool as well or record it as already-dead; either way it needs no build gate, because the tool cannot build regardless.



## Section 142 -- COMPLETED: transport-free safebox and mall item-transfer codec

**Scope.** One new transport-free protocol module, `protocol/src/cg_safebox.rs`, plus exactly one `pub mod cg_safebox;` line in `protocol/src/lib.rs`. No other source file changed. `protocol/src/cg_inventory.rs` and `protocol/src/cg_wire.rs` were **not** modified, because the active inventory had already resolved headers 69, 70, and 71 to a fixed eight-byte frame, so this slice required no framing change. The legacy server and client trees are untouched.

**Wire contract.** Active profile, **8 bytes** total, **7-byte** framed payload:

```text
offset 0      header        0x45 (69), 0x46 (70), or 0x47 (71)
offset 1..5   container_pos explicit little-endian u32
offset 5      window_type   opaque byte
offset 6..8   cell          explicit little-endian u16
```

Rust surface: `CgSafeBoxItem { kind: SafeBoxKind, container_pos: u32, item_pos: CgItemPos }` with `new`, `encode`, `encode_into`, `to_frame`, `decode`, `decode_frame`, and `header()`; `SafeBoxKind` with `MallCheckout`, `SafeboxCheckin`, and `SafeboxCheckout` variants, plus `header()`, `ALL`, `from_header()`, and `is_deposit()`; the error enum carries `Truncated{needed,available}`, `LengthMismatch{expected,actual}`, and `InvalidHeader(u8)`; constants are `CG_SAFEBOX_PAYLOAD_SIZE = 7`, `CG_SAFEBOX_WIRE_SIZE = 8`, and `CG_SAFEBOX_LEGACY_WIRE_SIZE = 5`, the last documented but deliberately unproducible. The shared `CgItemPos` is reused and `CG_ITEM_POS_SIZE` is re-exported, so this is the fifth Rust codec to share one packed position layout. There is no second framer, no `#[repr(C)]` compatibility struct, no `unsafe`, and no gameplay policy.

**Three design decisions of record.** First, this is the **second** record in the series to store a header byte and the **first with three** legal values; the inbound handshake is the first, because it accepts `0xff` and `0xfc`, and the stored `SafeBoxKind` enum is closed so that no unencodable state exists. Second, the feature profile is a **compile-time constant**, not a run-time profile: one `#define` per tree, ten `#if` uses, zero `#undef`, and zero build-system mention, so the 5-byte shape needs a source edit and is unreachable, and only the 8-byte shape is implemented, which is deliberately different from the DB boot profile already modelled in this ledger. Third, both wire fields stay **opaque**: the `u32` is a flat container cell index that the legacy container rejects rather than clamps, and `window_type` is never range-checked by the server, so borrowing `SItemPos::IsValidItemPosition` would have rejected every legitimate use of this record.

**Tests and mutation strength.** 14 tests in the new module, taking the protocol crate from 304 to 318 unit tests. **Seventeen mutations were applied and seventeen were caught**, with the source restored byte-for-byte after each: the seven recorded during implementation, the ten from the independent review including the one that had previously **survived**, and three added afterwards to pin the opacity claims, namely a `window_type` allowlist in the raw decoder, one in the framed decoder, and clamping `container_pos` to 269.

**Independent review: PASS**, no BLOCKER and no MAJOR, at `/tmp/agent-reports/cg_safebox_review.md`. The reviewer re-verified the size, the unreachable profile, the headers, all three collisions, the direction fact, the absence of clamping, the decoder precedence, the closed enum, and the reuse contract; it also **withdrew its own earlier clippy blocker** after re-measuring on a fresh scratch copy. All six of its findings were fixed: four were real errors in my own documentation, one was an untested public accessor that was fixed by making both encoders use it and adding a test, and one was a style divergence from the house pattern. Two further loose citations were tightened.
