## 166. MACHINE-DERIVED WIDTHS, AND THE GAME-TO-CLIENT RECORDS WITH NAMED FIELDS

### 166.1 What this batch covers

`protocol/src/gc_fields.rs` implements 18 game-to-client records that carry
named scalar fields and raw fixed `char` arrays. Fourteen Rust types cover the
18 headers, because six headers share layouts with another header:

| shared type | width | headers | byte values |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `GcNamed` | 30 | `ITEM_OWNERSHIP`, `PARTY_ADD`, `CHANGE_NAME` | 31, 78, 107 |
| `GcTwoWord` | 9 | `OWNERSHIP`, `PARTY_LINK`, `PARTY_UNLINK` | 62, 91, 92 |

The remaining twelve types each back one header. The module holds 39 unit tests
and adds seven public wiring tests, so `protocol/tests/cg_wiring.rs` grew from
49 to 56.

| record | width | record | width |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `PLAYER_POINTS` (16) | 2041 | `SHOP_SIGN` (39) | 38 |
| `PVP` (41) | 10 | `QUEST_CONFIRM` (46) | 74 |
| `AUTO_SHAMAN_SKILL` (57) | 10 | `PICKUP_ITEM_SC` (64) | 9 |
| `CREATE_FLY` (70) | 10 | `TARGET_UPDATE` (123) | 13 |
| `LOVER_INFO` (131) | 27 | `SPECIFIC_EFFECT` (208) | 133 |
| `CHARACTER_GOLD` (224) | 9 | | |

### 166.2 Every width here is machine-derived, not hand-summed

Section 163.7 recorded that the automated width calculator matched only three of
eight hand-summed ground truths, and section 165 hand-summed a further twenty
widths. This section replaces hand-summing with a measurement, and it works on
this host.

The host is 64-bit only, and `gcc -m32` is not available: `gcc-multilib` has no
installation candidate in this image. The working toolchain is
`gcc-12-multilib-i686-linux-gnu`, installed with `apt-get`, which provides
`i686-linux-gnu-g++-12`.

The probe, at `/tmp/wprobe.cpp`, does four things:

1. Copies the typedefs verbatim from `server/server/libthecore/typedef.h`,
   taking the `#ifndef __WIN32__` branch that the legacy FreeBSD server uses.
   That header fixes `DWORD = unsigned int`, `BYTE = unsigned char`,
   `WORD = unsigned short`, `LONG = long`, `ULONG = unsigned long`.
2. Copies each struct body verbatim out of both `Packet.h` files, substituting
   only the resolved array-dimension constants.
3. Wraps the set in `#pragma pack(push,1)`, which is what the legacy headers use.
4. Compiles with `-static` and prints `sizeof` for each type under i686.

`-static` is required. A default dynamic 32-bit link produces a binary that
cannot run, because the image has no `/lib/ld-linux.so.2`. That failure mode is
silent unless the run is checked: the compile succeeds and only the run fails.

**Two controls run with every batch.** First, five already-settled records from
sections 164 and 165 reproduce their earlier hand-summed widths exactly: 10, 9,
11, 13, and 5. Second, a packed struct of two C++ `long`s measures 8 bytes,
which proves the probe really is 32-bit and not an LP64 reading. Without that
second control a silently 64-bit probe would agree with a hand sum on records
containing no `long` and disagree only on the ones that do.

**All 18 records agree between the client-derived and server-derived bodies.**

### 166.3 A constant can be defined in four different ways, and a `#define` search misses three of them

This is the most reusable finding in the section, and it nearly produced a false
negative in this very section.

Resolving `CHARACTER_NAME_MAX_LEN` first appeared to fail. A whole-tree search
for `#define CHARACTER_NAME_MAX_LEN` returned **zero** definitions, while the
name appeared 143 times as a use. The correct definition is:

```c
/* server/server/common/length.h:15, inside an anonymous enum */
CHARACTER_NAME_MAX_LEN	= 24,
```

and on the client at `client/Client/UserInterface/StdAfx.h:43`. A constant may
be defined in at least four forms in this tree:

| form | example | file |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `#define NAME n` | `MAX_EFFECT_FILE_NAME` = 128 | `server/server/game/packet.h:2739` |
| `const T NAME = n;` | `ITEM_POS_MAX_NUM` and similar | `server/server/game/constants.h` |
| anonymous-enum member on its own line | `CHARACTER_NAME_MAX_LEN = 24,` | `server/server/common/length.h:15` |
| single-line named enum | `enum { LOGIN_STATUS_MAX_LEN = 8 };` | `client/Client/UserInterface/Packet.h:1131` |

A resolver must accept all four, and a search that accepts only the first
reports a symbol that is used 143 times as **not existing in the repository**.
That is the same failure class as the `--include=*.h` defect in section 163.1:
a search too narrow for the tree invents an absence.

The values that this batch depends on, all agreeing on both sides:

| constant | value | client | server |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `CHARACTER_NAME_MAX_LEN` | 24 | `StdAfx.h:43` | `common/length.h:15` |
| `SHOP_SIGN_MAX_LEN` | 32 | `Packet.h:249` | `common/length.h:16` |
| `MAX_EFFECT_FILE_NAME` | 128 | literal `128` | `packet.h:2739` |
| `POINT_MAX_NUM` | 255 | `StdAfx.h:42` | `common/length.h:81` |

### 166.4 Five array-dimension constants are genuinely absent from the tree

Having a working resolver, all 43 array-dimension constants used by the two
`Packet.h` files were checked. Five have **no definition anywhere** in
`server/` or `client/`, across all four forms:

| constant | uses | affects |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ITEM_ATTRIBUTE_MAX_NUM` | 77 | item attribute arrays |
| `ITEM_ATTRIBUTE_SLOT_MAX_NUM` | 35 | item attribute slots |
| `PRIVATE_SHOP_HOST_ITEM_MAX_NUM` | 27 | private shop host items |
| `CHR_EQUIPPART_NUM` | 11 | `awPart[CHR_EQUIPPART_NUM]` in two records |
| `ITEM_APPLY_RANDOM_SLOT_MAX_NUM` | 5 | random apply slots |

This is a real gap in the checked-in tree, not a search artifact. It was
confirmed with a bare `grep -rnI` for each name and by inspecting every hit:
the only definition-shaped lines are `extern const int aiItemAttributeAddPercent[ITEM_ATTRIBUTE_MAX_NUM]`
declarations, which are uses, not definitions.

Two consequences, both recorded rather than worked around:

- The translation units that use these constants cannot compile as checked in.
  The legacy tree is incomplete here.
- **Any record whose array dimension is one of these five has no
  source-derivable width.** Their widths must not be invented. This is now a
  documented blocked set, and such records are excluded from the batches below.

None of the 18 records in this batch depends on a missing constant, so this
section is unaffected by the gap.

### 166.5 Three field widths that depend on the 32-bit target

`server/server/premake5.lua:12` sets `architecture "x86"`. The probe confirms
the consequences rather than assuming them:

- `TPacketGCQuestConfirm.timeout` is a C++ `long` and measures **4** bytes, so
  the record is 74 and not 78.
- `TPacketGCTargetUpdate.lID`, `.lX`, and `.lY` are C++ `long` and measure 4
  bytes each, so the record is 13 and not 21.
- `TPacketGCPoints.points` is `long long` at 8 bytes, so the record is
  `1 + 255 * 8 = 2041`. `TPacketGCGold.gold` is `unsigned long long` at 8
  bytes, so it is 9.

`TPacketGCTargetUpdate` is written `long lX, lY;`, a **two-declarator field on
one line**. A parser that assumes one field per line reads that record as two
fields and computes 9 bytes instead of 13.

There is a trap in the same legacy header. `QWORD` and `ULONG` are
`unsigned long`, which is **4** bytes on this target, not 8. `QWORD` is
misleadingly named. No record in this module uses it, but any future record that
does must be measured, not assumed.

### 166.6 A record the server sends through a differently named struct

`HEADER_GC_MOTION` (36) is a client `TPacketGCMotion` and a server
`struct packet_motion`, declared with the plain `struct NAME { ... };` form.
`char.cpp:5045` takes it as a pointer parameter:

```c
void CHARACTER::MotionPacketEncode(BYTE motion, LPCHARACTER victim, struct packet_motion * packet)
```

The two bodies are identical, and the probe measured 11 from both.

`HEADER_GC_PARTY_UNLINK` (92) has a related shape. The server **does** declare
`TPacketGCPartyUnlink`, but it never sends it. `party.cpp:729` sends the unlink
record as a `TPacketGCPartyLink` with only the header byte changed:

```c
TPacketGCPartyLink p;
p.header = HEADER_GC_PARTY_UNLINK;
```

So the unlink record is reached through the link type. This is the third
game-to-client instance, after `HEADER_CG_FLY_TARGETING` in section 161 and
`TPacketGCItemDel` in section 165, of a record whose header is the only thing
distinguishing it from another record of the same struct. The test
`the_header_byte_is_the_only_thing_separating_the_three_named_records` pins that
all three headers stay distinct.

### 166.7 The server's struct definitions are not confined to `packet.h`

A search restricted to `server/server/game/packet.h` reported five of the 18
records as **client-only**: `Motion`, `ShamanUseSkill`, `PickupItemSC`,
`PartyLink`, and `PartyUnlink`. That was wrong. All five have server
definitions, either under a different name (`packet_motion`) or in a header
outside the searched file. Widening the root to all of `server/server` found
every one, and the probe then measured matching widths for all of them.

A struct search over a subset of the tree produces the same class of false
absence as the narrow constant resolver in section 166.3.

### 166.8 One feature gate that resolves

`HEADER_GC_AUTO_SHAMAN_SKILL` (57) is sent from `char.cpp:12745` inside
`#ifdef __ENABLE_SHAMAN_SYSTEM__`. That macro **is** defined on both sides, at
`server/server/common/prodomodefines.h:193` and
`client/Client/UserInterface/LOCALE_INC.H:143`, so the record is live and its
width does not vary.

The send site also uses aggregate initialisation, which independently confirms
the field order:

```c
TPacketGCShamanUseSkill pack {HEADER_GC_AUTO_SHAMAN_SKILL, dwSkillVnum, GetVID(), byLevel };
```

No record in this batch sits behind a profile that is undefined, so no record
here has two possible widths. This is the first batch where that is true of
every member.

### 166.9 A field name that lies about its own width

`TPacketGCShamanUseSkill` declares its last field as `dwLevel`, which the `dw`
prefix makes look like a `DWORD`. It is declared `BYTE`, and the probe measures
the record at **10** bytes, not 13. The Rust field is `level: u8` and the test
`the_shaman_skill_level_is_one_byte_not_a_word` pins the 10-byte width and the
single trailing byte.

`CHARACTER_NAME_MAX_LEN` has the same shape: `CHARACTER_NAME_MAX_LEN` reads
like a maximum, but the records use `CHARACTER_NAME_MAX_LEN + 1`, so the wire
field is 25 bytes and holds a NUL-terminated string whose longest name is 24
characters. The codec keeps the whole 25 bytes as raw storage and does not
validate the terminator.

### 166.10 Signedness that differs between two records in one module

`GcPoints.points` is `long long` and is `i64`. `GcGold.gold` is
`unsigned long long` and is `u64`. The two records look alike on the wire, at
eight bytes per value, but their high bits mean opposite things. The test
`the_gold_and_points_records_use_opposite_signedness` checks `i64::MIN` and
`u64::MAX` in the same test so the distinction cannot be quietly lost.

`GcPickupItem` uses C++ `int` and is `i32`, so a negative count round-trips as
negative rather than as a huge unsigned value.

### 166.11 Mutation evidence, and eight real coverage gaps the first round found

Two rounds were run on `gc_fields.rs`, each mutation applied to the pristine
file so the results are independent.

Round one, 16 mutations of constants and slice bounds: 16 of 16 caught, but 11
were compile errors, so the tests never ran for them. That is weak evidence and
it is recorded as such.

Round two, 31 mutations that all compile: 15 byte-order reversals, three
`header()` substitutions, seven field-index shifts, four header-field index
shifts, and two encoder header suppressions. **23 of 31 caught, 8 survivors.**

All eight survivors were **real coverage gaps**, not equivalent mutants:

| survivor | cause |
| --- | --- |
| `GcPvp.source` big-endian | no test read the field back |
| `GcPvp.target` big-endian | no test read the field back |
| `GcMotion.motion` big-endian | only `u16::MAX` was used, which is byte-symmetric |
| `GcShamanSkill.skill_vnum` big-endian | no test read the field back |
| `GcShopSign.vid` big-endian | no test read the field back |
| `GcCreateFly.start_vid` index shift | encode-only, no decode round trip |
| `GcShamanSkill.vid` index shift | encode-only, no decode round trip |
| `GcMotion.victim_vid` index shift | encode-only, no decode round trip |

Three records were tested on the encode side only, and the tests that did decode
used values whose two halves were equal, so a byte reversal was invisible.

The fix was three new tests, not suppressions:

- `every_scalar_record_decodes_back_to_every_field_it_was_built_with` and
  `every_array_record_decodes_back_to_every_field_it_was_built_with`, which
  read **every** field of **every** record back, using values with distinct
  halves and a `ramp` generator so no test value can be byte-symmetric.
- `no_two_adjacent_fields_of_any_record_are_interchangeable`, which encodes each
  adjacent pair both ways round and confirms the two frames differ.
- `no_multi_byte_field_survives_a_byte_reversal`, which reverses a whole frame
  and requires the decode to differ.

All eight mutations are now caught. Two of the three new tests were then
refactored to satisfy Clippy, splitting one 243-line test into two and replacing
narrowing casts with a `ramp` iterator, and all eight mutations were re-run
against the refactored tests and still caught.

Total for the section: 47 mutations, 47 caught, zero survivors, zero equivalent
mutants. `gc_fields.rs` was restored byte-for-byte after each round, confirmed by
SHA-256, and a debris scan found no `from_be_bytes` and no altered constant.

### 166.12 A defect in the first version of the sweep itself

The first sweep implementation built a cumulative buffer: each mutation was
applied on top of the previous one, so a reported "catch" might have come from an
earlier mutation rather than the one under test. The second implementation
rebuilds the file from the pristine source for every mutation, deduplicates
anchors so no two mutations share a target, and asserts that the mutated text
differs from the source before running.

This is recorded because the cumulative version reported 16 of 16 caught, which
looked like a stronger result than it was.

## Section 167 — implementation: the nested and fixed-array game-to-client records

This section implements the twelve fixed-size game-to-client records that the
Section 166 audit selected as the next tractable batch, and it closes the
`gc_fields` era in favour of records that embed a nested body or a fixed-length
array. The module is `protocol/src/gc_nested.rs`.

### 167.1 Records implemented

| wire byte | client name | legacy type | packed width | Rust type |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 17 | `HEADER_GC_PLAYER_POINT_CHANGE` | `TPacketGCPointChange` | 25 | `GcPointChange` |
| 65 | `HEADER_GC_WARP` | `TPacketGCWarp` | 15 | `GcWarp` |
| 69 | `HEADER_GC_ADD_FLY_TARGETING` | `TPacketGCFlyTargeting` | 17 | `GcFlyTargeting` |
| 71 | `HEADER_GC_FLY_TARGETING` | `TPacketGCFlyTargeting` | 17 | `GcFlyTargeting` |
| 76 | `HEADER_GC_SKILL_LEVEL_NEW` | `TPacketGCSkillLevelNew` | 1531 | `GcSkillLevelNew` |
| 79 | `HEADER_GC_PARTY_UPDATE` | `TPacketGCPartyUpdate` | 21 | `GcPartyUpdate` |
| 126 | `HEADER_GC_AFFECT_ADD` | `TPacketGCAffectAdd` | 22 | `GcAffectAdd` |
| 134 | `HEADER_GC_DIG_MOTION` | `TPacketGCDigMotion` | 10 | `GcDigMotion` |
| 135 | `HEADER_GC_DAMAGE_INFO` | `TPacketGCDamageInfo` | 10 | `GcDamageInfo` |
| 141 | `HEADER_GC_PREMIUM_PLAYERS` | `TPacketGCPremiumPlayers` | 28 | `GcPremiumPlayers` |
| 180 | `HEADER_GC_DAILY_GIFT` | `TPacketGCDailyGift` | 111 | `GcDailyGift` |
| 221 | `HEADER_GC_CUBE_RENEWAL` | `TPacketGCCubeRenewalReceive` | 171 | `GcCubeRenewal` |

Twelve headers and twelve rows, but only eleven legacy types, because bytes 69
and 71 share `TPacketGCFlyTargeting` and differ only in the header byte. The
shared body is one Rust type with a `header` field, and
`GC_FLY_TARGETING_HEADERS` names both bytes.

Three nested body types are also public and independently decodable:
`GcSkill` (6 bytes), `GcAffectElement` (21 bytes), and `GcCubeRenewalDate`
(169 bytes). The cube record is a header byte, a subheader byte, and one date.

### 167.2 Widths are machine-derived, and three of them surprise a hand sum

Every width was measured by compiling a verbatim packed reproduction with
`i686-linux-gnu-g++-12 -static`, the same method Section 166 established. The
positive controls were the known widths 10, 9, 11, 13, and 5, plus a packed
two-`long` struct that measured 8 bytes and so proves a 32-bit target.

Three widths disagree with what the declaration order suggests:

* **`GcDigMotion` is 10, not 14.** A hand sum of a header, two `DWORD`s, and a
  `BYTE` is 10 once the header is counted, but the record as written reads
  14 by mistake, and 14 is the value a reader would guess from a four-field
  64-bit mental model. The probe is what settles it.
* **`GcSkill` is 6, not 10.** `TPlayerSkill` is `{ BYTE bMasterType; BYTE
  bLevel; time_t tNextRead; }`. `time_t` is **4 bytes** on the legacy target,
  so the entry is 6 bytes. A 64-bit mental model gives 10 and would make the
  255-entry table 2551 bytes instead of 1531.
* **`GcPointChange` is 25.** Its `header` field is a 4-byte `int`, not a byte.
  Treating the header as a `u8` gives 22. The Rust type therefore carries
  `header: i32` and the decoder has no single-byte header check at all.

`GcWarp` is 15 because it is three 4-byte `long`s and one `WORD`. The server
declares `wPort` as a `WORD`, so the last field is 2 bytes, not 4.

### 167.3 The cube-renewal date interleaves its material pairs

This is the one real layout trap in the batch, and it is invisible to a width
check.

`TInfoDateCubeRenewal` declares its five material pairs **in pairs**, not as
two arrays:

```c
DWORD vnum_material_1;  int count_material_1;
DWORD vnum_material_2;  int count_material_2;
...
```

So the wire layout is `vnum_0, count_0, vnum_1, count_1, ...` and material
`i` sits at byte `17 + 8 * i`, with its count at `21 + 8 * i`. The Rust type
exposes two clean arrays, which invites an encoder that writes them as two
adjacent blocks.

**That is exactly the bug this section's own tests caught.** The first
implementation read the fields as two adjacent blocks. The record still
measured 169 bytes, so every width assertion, every round-trip through the
matching offset pair, and every published constant passed. The mismatch only
appeared when a record was built with the Rust arrays and read back, because
the decoder and the encoder were wrong in *mirrored* ways.

The fix is in both directions: the decoder strides 8 bytes and the encoder
interleaves. `the_cube_material_pairs_are_interleaved_on_the_wire` now pins
the exact bytes, including that byte 21 holds `count_material[0]` rather than
`vnum_material[1]`.

**Lesson recorded: a self-consistent codec with a wrong layout passes every
self-consistent test.** Width probes and mirror-image round trips are not
independent. Only golden bytes, or a source-order claim, can catch a layout
that is uniformly shifted.

### 167.4 Two skill-level generations share a header count but not a body

Byte 76 is the live record. Byte 72 is declared by both trees and sent by
neither:

* the client's `HEADER_GC_SKILL_LEVEL_NEW` (76) and the server's
  `HEADER_GC_SKILL_LEVEL` (76) both carry `TPlayerSkill skills[255]`, so both
  measure `1 + 255 * 6 = 1531` bytes;
* the client's byte-72 `TPacketGCSkillLevel` is a `BYTE[255]` body, 256 bytes;
* the server's byte-72 name is `HEADER_GC_SKILL_LEVEL_OLD`, and it has no
  struct body at all.

**The names are swapped between the trees.** The client calls the live record
`..._NEW` and the dead one plain; the server calls the live record plain and
the dead one `..._OLD`. The module is keyed to byte 76 and publishes
`GC_SKILL_LEVEL_NEW_WIRE_SIZE = 1531` and
`GC_SKILL_LEVEL_OLD_WIRE_SIZE = 256` as two different constants for two
different shapes. `the_skill_level_generations_keep_their_own_bodies` asserts
that a 256-byte frame is rejected by the live decoder, and that the two
constants never become equal.

### 167.5 Server and client disagree on the byte-17 name

The positive-control constant resolver, run over both trees for all twelve
headers, agreed on every value, and corrected one documentation error.

Byte 17 is `HEADER_GC_PLAYER_POINT_CHANGE` in the client and
`HEADER_GC_CHARACTER_POINT_CHANGE` in the server
(`server/server/game/packet.h:117`). An earlier draft of `gc.rs` claimed the
server "has no enumerator for this byte". It does, under a different name.
`gc.rs` now publishes `HEADER_GC_CHARACTER_POINT_CHANGE` and
`HEADER_GC_SKILL_LEVEL_SERVER` as aliases so the two trees can be compared by
name without a false second record appearing.

**The constant resolver found nothing for any of the twelve headers on its
first pass** when it searched only for `#define`. All twelve are
multiline anonymous-enum members:

```c
HEADER_GC_WARP                                        = 65,
```

This is the Section 152 lesson recurring exactly: a `#define`-only search
reports a false absence. All twelve values were re-verified with a resolver
that accepts `#define`, `const T NAME = value`, a multiline enum member, and a
single-line `enum { NAME = value }`, with a `#define` control and a
single-line-enum control.

### 167.6 A client-only constant, and a literal on the server

`PARTY_AFFECT_SLOT_MAX_NUM` is 7 in `client/Client/UserInterface/Packet.h`.
The server has no definition and writes the literal `7` into its own body. The
module documents this and publishes `GC_PARTY_AFFECT_SLOT_COUNT = 7`. This is
a case where the client definition is the only source for the array bound and
the server agrees by coincidence of literal, not by sharing a name.

By contrast, `DAILY_GIFT_WEEK_DAYS` is 7 on both sides and is shared.

### 167.8 Mutation sweep

**53 mutations**, every one applied independently to the pristine source and
then restored. The sweep never accumulates: each mutation is
`pristine.replace(old, new, 1)`, the file is written, `cargo test -p protocol
--lib` runs, and the result is recorded before the next mutation starts from
the pristine text again.

| verdict | count | meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `CAUGHT` | 49 | a test failed, so the mutation is detected |
| `COMPILE_ERROR` | 2 | rejected by the type system, weak evidence |
| `SURVIVED` | 2 | proved equivalent, not a coverage gap |
| **total** | **53** | |

The 53 mutations fall into nine classes:

* **A, 3 reader byte order.** `u32_at`, `i32_at`, and `i64_at` from
  big-endian instead of little-endian.
* **B, 5 encoder byte order.** The `time_t` word, `GcWarp::port`,
  `GcCubeRenewalDate::gold`, `npc_vnum`, and `vnum_reward` from big-endian.
* **C, 14 field index shifts.** Adjacent-field swaps in the point change, warp
  `x`/`y`/`addr`, dig-motion `target_vid`/`count`, the `time_t`, the affect SP
  cost, the cube `gold` and `percent`, and the party's `state`/`percent_hp`;
  plus offset shifts in the premium name, the party affects, the daily-gift
  `count`, `collect_time`, and `cost`, a `status` read strided by two, and a
  `cost` value that is XORed with `0xffff`.
* **D, 3 the cube interleaving.** Two adjacent blocks instead of interleaved
  pairs, a block-strided read, and a four-pair read. All three are the Section
  167.3 bug reproduced as mutants.
* **E, 3 header substitutions.** Warp keyed to the fly header, damage keyed to
  the dig header, skill level keyed to the dead byte 72.
* **F, 4 header validation removals.** Three `check_header` calls deleted, and
  `check_header` itself made to never return an error.
* **H, 7 width constants.** Daily gift 111 to 104, point change 25 to 21, fly
  17 to 13, skill slot count 255 to 254, party affect count 7 to 8, cube
  category 100 to 99, and skill 6 to 10, which is the 64-bit `time_t` mistake.
* **I, 5 structural.** The fly header byte not pushed, daily-gift cash and
  week swapped, award vnum and count swapped, affect duration and apply value
  swapped, status written as `u16`.
* **J, 9 signedness.** Seven *converting* reads (`abs` on the award
  `count_reward`, the `time_t`, the cube `count_reward` and `count_material`,
  the point-change `amount`, and the affect `duration`; a saturating fold on
  the warp `x`; a wrapping division on the award `gold`) and two
  *reinterpreting* reads (the award `count_reward` and the `time_t` as
  `u32_at(..) as i32`).

Class `G` is unused: the length-check mutation was dropped because the
`take` helper has no single-anchor form, and a `needed = 0` substitution would
have failed to compile rather than testing anything. The nine letters used are
A, B, C, D, E, F, H, I, and J.

Restoration was hash-verified. The pre-sweep and post-sweep SHA-256 of
`gc_nested.rs` are both
`b84d647c5c067d41c63b033b325b80ffb3a7f413ac9417eadb37ebfbbae33067`, and the
file is byte-for-byte the pristine text. A debris scan for `from_be_bytes`,
`min(i32::MAX`, `abs()` in the new module, `saturating_sub`,
`todo!`, `unimplemented!`, and `dbg!` found no mutation residue.

### 167.9 The two survivors are provable equivalents, and they still taught us something

Both survivors are the same reinterpreting signedness mutation:

```rust
count_reward: u32_at(raw, 12) as i32,   // survivor
count_reward: i32_at(raw, 12),          // pristine
```

Rust defines `u32 as i32` as a wrapping two's-complement bit reinterpretation,
and `i32::from_le_bytes` is that same reinterpretation of the same four bytes.
The two expressions are **identical for every possible input**, not merely
equal on the tested inputs. This was checked empirically over 200,012 values
including every boundary: 0, 1, 255, 256, `0x7fffffff`, `0x80000000`,
`0xffffffff`, `0x80000001`, and 200,000 pseudorandom words, with zero
disagreements.

These are equivalent mutants, not coverage gaps, and the right response is to
record them as such rather than to contrive a test that "catches" a no-op.

**But the pair still exposed a real gap.** An equivalent mutant proves the
tests cannot tell a *reinterpreting* read from another reinterpreting read. It
says nothing about a *converting* read, which is a different defect. So four
boundary tests were added that a converting read cannot pass:

* `the_signed_fields_keep_their_full_32_bit_range` walks `i32::MIN`, `-65537`,
  `-1`, `0`, `1`, `255`, `65536`, and `i32::MAX` through the affect duration,
  the affect SP cost, the damage, and the warp `x`;
* `the_point_change_long_longs_keep_their_full_64_bit_range` walks
  `i64::MIN` through `i64::MAX`, using the complement as the paired value so
  the two `long long` fields cannot both saturate to the same thing;
* `the_cube_material_counts_stay_signed` puts one negative extreme in all five
  `count_material` slots and checks `count_reward` is untouched;
* `the_skill_time_t_keeps_its_signed_range` checks the negative half of the
  `time_t` range, both for one entry and for all 255 table slots.

Seven new signedness mutations were then added to the plan, covering `abs`, a
saturating fold to `i32::MAX`, and a wrapping division. **All seven are caught
by the four new tests.** The final tally is the table in 167.8.

The two compile-error kills were also read rather than accepted as evidence.
`E_skill_level header is dead byte 72` fails with `E0425: cannot find value
HEADER_GC_SKILL_LEVEL in this scope`, because the module deliberately imports
only `HEADER_GC_SKILL_LEVEL_NEW`. `H_party_affect_count 8` fails with
`E0308: mismatched types` in the test literals, because the array length is a
type parameter. Both are name- and type-level rejections, so both are reported
as weak evidence rather than as semantic kills.

### 167.10 Lint failures were fixed by refactoring, never by suppression

Five Clippy findings in the new tests were fixed structurally:

* `error: casting usize to u8 may truncate the value` in `sample_skill`.
  Replaced with `u8::try_from(index % 256)` and `u16::try_from(index % 512)`.
* `error: casting usize to u32 may truncate the value` in the daily-gift array
  filler. Replaced with `u32::try_from(index)`.
* `error: casting u32 to i32 may wrap around the value` for `BIG_TIME_T`.
  Replaced with `i32::MIN.wrapping_add(0x1122_3344)`, which is *more*
  adversarial than the cast it replaced, because the literal is not a valid
  positive `i32`.
* `error: this argument is passed by value, but not consumed` for the `check`
  helper. Changed to take `&[u8]`, and all eleven call sites updated.
* `error: this function has too many lines` twice: a 169-line round-trip test
  split into a scalar group and an array group, and a 101-line test that kept
  coming back over the limit split again so the two ten-byte records live in
  `the_two_ten_byte_records_round_trip_to_every_field`.
* `error: variable does not need to be mutable` for a test-local `GcSkill`.
  The `mut` was removed.

No `#[allow]` attribute was added to the new module.

### 167.13 Still blocked, and deliberately deferred

Two records examined during this section were **not** implemented, and both
reasons are load-bearing:

* **`TPacketGCExchange`** is blocked by the genuinely undefined

* **`TPacketGCMount`** has **no server send site** in the checked-in tree. It
  is client-registered, but no producer exists, so there is no server body to
  cross-check a client width against. Section 165 found the same pattern for
  five other bytes (18, 73, 84, 112, 213).

this work. They need real nested or subheader dispatch, and `HEADER_GG_GUILD`
in the game-to-game direction needs the same. Those are designed separately.


### 167.14 Correction to Section 166.4: four of the five "absent" constants are present

Section 166.4 recorded five array-dimension constants as having no definition
anywhere in the tree. **Four of the five are defined.** Section 166.4's
resolver accepted a numeric literal after `=`, and the four are defined in forms
it therefore could not read:

| constant | value | definition | why Section 166.4 missed it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ITEM_ATTRIBUTE_MAX_NUM` | 7 | `server/server/common/item_length.h:30` = `ITEM_ATTRIBUTE_RARE_END` | the value is an **expression**, not a literal |
| `ITEM_ATTRIBUTE_SLOT_MAX_NUM` | 7 | `client/Client/UserInterface/GameType.h:566` = `ITEM_ATTRIBUTE_NORM_NUM + ITEM_ATTRIBUTE_RARE_NUM` | the value is an **expression** |
| `PRIVATE_SHOP_HOST_ITEM_MAX_NUM` | 128 | `client/.../Packet.h:290` and `server/.../common/length.h:136` = `(PRIVATE_SHOP_WIDTH * PRIVATE_SHOP_HEIGHT) * PRIVATE_SHOP_PAGE_MAX_NUM` | the value is an **expression** |
| `CHR_EQUIPPART_NUM` | 6 | `client/.../Packet.h` enum `ECharacterEquipmentPart`, last member | the member has **no `=` at all**; it is auto-incremented |

Only `ITEM_APPLY_RANDOM_SLOT_MAX_NUM` is genuinely absent: it is used five
times (`client/.../Packet.h:3513,3546` and three private-shop sites) and never
defined.

**The resolver defect is the same class as the two already recorded.** A
`#define`-only search invented an absence in Section 163.1. A
`numeric-literal-only` resolver invented one here. A constant resolver must
accept: `#define NAME n`, `const T NAME = n`, a literal-valued enum member, an
**expression-valued** enum member over other constants, and an
**auto-incremented** member with no `=`.

**The values are machine-derived, not hand-summed.** A verbatim reproduction
was compiled with `i686-linux-gnu-g++-12 -static` and reports:

```
CHR_EQUIPPART_NUM             = 6
ITEM_ATTRIBUTE_MAX_NUM        = 7
ITEM_ATTRIBUTE_SLOT_MAX_NUM   = 7
PRIVATE_SHOP_HOST_ITEM_MAX_NUM= 128
```

The `item_length.h:30` source comment `// 7` agrees with the compiled value, and
`ITEM_ATTRIBUTE_NORM_NUM = 5` plus `ITEM_ATTRIBUTE_RARE_NUM = 2` gives the same
7 on both trees.

`CHR_EQUIPPART_NUM` is **gate-dependent**, and the negative control proves it.
With `ENABLE_SASH_SYSTEM` and `ENABLE_AURA_SYSTEM` both active the enum is
`ARMOR, WEAPON, HEAD, HAIR, SASH, AURA, NUM` and the value is **6**. With both
gates off it is `ARMOR, WEAPON, HEAD, HAIR, NUM` and the value is **4**. The
active client profile is the one that matters, and it gives 6.

This unblocks `TPacketGCExchange` (byte 42) and the two records that declare
`awPart[CHR_EQUIPPART_NUM]`, one of which is byte 136
`HEADER_GC_CHAR_ADDITIONAL_INFO`. Section 167.13's claim that
`TPacketGCExchange` "is blocked by the genuinely undefined
`ITEM_ATTRIBUTE_SLOT_MAX_NUM`" is **withdrawn as wrong**.

## Section 168 — implementation: the actor, target, and main-character game-to-client records

This section implements the 14 fixed-size game-to-client records that carry
character appearance, position, targeting, and own-character state. They are
`protocol/src/gc_actors.rs`, registered in `protocol/src/lib.rs`, and their
inventory rows in `protocol/src/gc_inventory.rs` are now marked
`implemented_in_rust: true`.

**The class splits 3 dead client entries and 11 live pairs.** Section 167.13
left these as the next safe boundary because each one is a `#pragma pack(1)`
struct under a wide feature-gate set. That is true, and it is also why the
widths could not be hand-summed.

### 168.1 The 14 records, their headers, and their measured widths

No width below is hand-summed. Each was derived by extracting the struct body
verbatim from `client/Client/UserInterface/Packet.h`, substituting the resolved
array-dimension constants, applying the complete active gate set, and compiling
the result with `i686-linux-gnu-g++-12` for `sizeof`.

| 15 | `HEADER_GC_MAIN_CHARACTER` | `HEADER_GC_MAIN_CHARACTER_OLD` | `TPacketGCMainCharacter` | 45 |
| 19 | `HEADER_GC_CHARACTER_UPDATE` | same | `TPacketGCCharacterUpdate` | 55 |
| 58 | `HEADER_GC_TARGET_INFO` | same | `TPacketGCTargetInfo` | 19 |

The C++ type column is the **client** spelling, which is the side this module
models. The server spells four of the same records differently:
`TPacketGCMainCharacter3BGM` and `TPacketGCMainCharacter4BGMVol` become
`TPacketGCMainCharacter3_BGM` and `TPacketGCMainCharacter4_BGM_VOL`, byte 136
uses the same `TPacketGCCharacterAdditionalInfo`, and byte 225 is
`TPacketGCGoldChange` on both sides. The Rust names follow the client.

### 168.2 Two widths that a hand sum gets wrong

**`GcTarget` is 32 bytes, and byte 58 is 19, not 33.** The target name array
is `TARGET_NAME_LEN = 33`, not 25, so `TPacketGCTargetInfo` and
`TPacketGCTargetCreateNew` cannot share a "name field" with the character-name
records. Three distinct name lengths are in play:

| constant | value | defined as |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `CHARACTER_NAME_MAX_LEN` | 24 | `client/.../StdAfx.h:43`, `server/.../common/length.h:15` |
| `CHR_EQUIPPART_NUM` | 6 | auto-incremented last member of `ECharacterEquipmentPart` |
| `SKILL_MAX_NUM` | 255 | `#define` in `client/.../Packet.h:2136`, enum member in `server/.../common/length.h` |

so the client and server arrays are 25, 25, and 33 bytes.

**`CHR_EQUIPPART_NUM` is gate-dependent.** With `ENABLE_SASH_SYSTEM` and
`ENABLE_AURA_SYSTEM` both active the enumeration is
`ARMOR, WEAPON, HEAD, HAIR, SASH, AURA, NUM`, which is **6**. A negative
control compiled with both gates off measures **4**. Byte 136 is therefore a
`[u16; 6]` that is only correct for the active profile, and the module says so.

`SKILL_MAX_NUM = 255` is the reason byte 72 is 256 bytes rather than 260: the
array is 255 bytes and the header is 1.

### 168.3 The server packing is a bare `#pragma pack(1)`

`server/server/common/tables.h` sets packing with a **bare**
`#pragma pack(1)` and no matching `pop`. A push-minus-pop heuristic therefore
reports a mismatch and the "unpacked" widths are wrong. Under the correct
reading `SPlayerSkill` is **6 bytes**, not 8, and the live byte-76 skill record
is **1531** bytes, not 1275 or 2041. That record is already covered by
`protocol::gc_nested`; byte 72 is the dead complementary generation, not a
duplicate of it.

### 168.4 The side-specific header names, and the three dead client entries

Resolving each enumerator against the real send sites **withdrew an earlier
"defect" conclusion**. The previous reading compared unrelated generations and
called bytes 15 and 72 protocol defects. They are not.

| byte | server declaration | server send site | verdict |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 15 | `HEADER_GC_MAIN_CHARACTER_OLD` | **none** | dead client decode entry |
| 72 | `HEADER_GC_SKILL_LEVEL_OLD` | **none** | dead client decode entry |
| 113 | `HEADER_GC_MAIN_CHARACTER` | `server/server/game/char.cpp:2018` | live pair, 46 = 46 |
| 117 | **no enumerator** | **none** | dead client decode entry |
| 125 | `HEADER_GC_TARGET_CREATE` | `server/server/game/target.cpp:22` | live pair |
| 225 | `HEADER_GC_CHARACTER_GOLD_CHANGE` | `server/server/game/char.cpp:3848` | live pair |

So **three** of the 14 are client decode entries the checked-in server never
produces — [`GcMainCharacter`] (byte 15), [`GcSkillLevel`] (byte 72), and
[`GcCharacterUpdate2`] (byte 117) — and the other **11** are live pairs whose
client and server structs agree on every field offset. None of the 14 is a
protocol defect.

Bytes 113 and 125 are ordinary matching pairs that merely carry different
names on the two sides, so they are not defects either.

### 168.5 Byte 225 has a four-byte header

`TPacketGCGoldChange` declares `DWORD header;` and is sent as the
little-endian value `0x000000e1`. It is the only four-byte header in this
module, and it is the reason the module has one special case: the decoder reads
four little-endian bytes and compares the whole word, and
`the_gold_header_is_checked_across_all_four_bytes` corrupts each of the four
bytes in turn to prove the check is not partial.

The client spells this record in a **second guarded `enum`** at
`client/.../Packet.h:3047`, not in the main table.

### 168.6 Codec design

- **Headers are canonical, not caller-mutable.** No record struct has a header
  field. `encode_into` writes the record's own fixed header, matching the
  existing `gc_fields` convention, and every constructor takes only non-header
  fields. A caller cannot build a record its own decoder would reject.
- **Field order and widths are explicit.** Each decoder reads byte ranges
  directly; there are no packed Rust structs.
- **A private `array::<N>` helper replaces 31 `expect` sites.** Every decoder
  calls `take` first, which proves the buffer is exactly the record's wire
  size, so each field slice is in range. Replacing
  `raw[a..b].try_into().expect(...)` and the manual `from_le_bytes([raw[i],
  ...])` index soup with one infeasible-failure `array` helper removed the last
  panicking path from the decoders. This was a refactor, not a suppression.
- **Float-containing records derive only `PartialEq`.** `GcCharacterAdd` and
  `GcMainCharacter4BgmVol` contain `f32`; deriving `Eq` on them does not
  compile.
- **Raw `char` arrays stay raw.** Embedded NULs and high bytes are preserved
  byte for byte; no name is trimmed, validated, or interpreted.

### 168.7 Tests

`protocol/src/gc_actors.rs` has a table-driven internal test module. One
`Rec` row per record carries the legacy name, the Rust type name, the header,
the wire size, a `sample` constructor, and a single `round_trip` hook. The
single hook covers every case: `Ok` means accepted, and comparing the result
with the input is a byte-for-byte round trip.

The sample values are chosen so **no two adjacent fields share a value**, which
is what lets the swap and reversal tests notice a wrong field order or byte
order.

| test | what it proves |
| --- | --- |
| `every_record_encodes_to_its_declared_wire_size` | declared width, header first |
| `every_record_round_trips_byte_for_byte` | decode then re-encode is identity |
| `a_second_round_trip_changes_nothing` | decoding is a fixed point |
| `every_record_rejects_every_truncated_prefix` | all 32 prefix lengths per record |
| `every_record_rejects_a_wrong_header` | rejection is a `Header` error, not a panic |
| `all_fourteen_headers_are_distinct` | no two records can be confused |
| `no_record_accepts_another_records_bytes` | 182 cross-record pairs |
| `no_two_adjacent_fields_of_any_record_are_interchangeable` | field order is observable |
| `no_record_survives_a_full_byte_reversal` | byte order is observable |
| `the_gold_header_is_checked_across_all_four_bytes` | the four-byte header check |
| `the_three_dead_client_entries_keep_their_measured_widths` | 45, 256, 44 |
| `the_live_main_character_record_is_byte_113` | 15 is not the live record |
| `the_three_name_array_lengths_stay_distinct` | 25, 25, 33 never unified |
| `raw_name_arrays_preserve_every_byte_including_nul` | NUL and high bytes survive |
| `the_resolved_array_constants_match_the_legacy_values` | 24, 6, 255 |

`protocol/tests/cg_wiring.rs` adds five public-surface tests: all 14 headers
resolve to their legacy bytes, all 14 measured widths, the three name lengths,
the four-byte gold header, and the inventory marking all 14 rows implemented.

## 169. TOML configuration for both binaries (M1, owner decision 2)

This section implements milestone M1's configuration half and owner decision 2 from
`docs/STATUS.md`: both binaries are configured by TOML, the legacy `key=value` parsers in
`common/src/config.rs` are replaced, and the legacy `CONFIG` and `conf.txt` files are no longer
read. It does **not** land the database half of M1; that is recorded as still open in 169.9.

### 169.1 What changed

| file | change |
|---|---|
| `Cargo.toml` | added `toml = "0.8"` to `[workspace.dependencies]`. |

| `Cargo.lock` | `toml 0.8.23`, `toml_edit 0.22.27`, `toml_datetime 0.6.11`, `serde_spanned 0.6.9`, `toml_write 0.1.2`, `winnow 0.7.15`. Added with a single online `cargo fetch`; every gate afterwards ran `--locked --offline`. |
| `common/src/config.rs` | `parse_game_config` and `parse_db_config` now deserialize TOML. The hand-written `parse_bool`, `parse_int_list`, `parse_string_list`, `parse_sql_config`, `parse_db_sql_config`, `parse_adminpage_ips`, and `parse_config_content` helpers are deleted. `GameConfig`, `DbConfig`, and `SqlConfig` derive `Serialize`/`Deserialize` and are `PartialEq`/`Eq`. |
| `common/tests/config_test.rs` | rewritten: 13 legacy-format tests replaced by 19 TOML tests. |
| `game-server/src/main.rs` | default path `CONFIG` -> `game.toml`; help text updated. |

| `README.md` | new "Configuration" section; run commands use `game.toml` / `db.toml`. |

The two function names, `parse_game_config` and `parse_db_config`, are kept so the binaries'
call sites did not change. Only the error type changed, from `String` to `ConfigError`.

### 169.2 Schema

Scalar settings stay **top-level TOML keys named after the Rust field**. Only the three SQL
connections of each binary become sub-tables:

| binary | sub-tables |
|---|---|
| `game-server` | `[player_sql]`, `[common_sql]`, `[log_sql]` |
| `db-server` | `[sql_player]`, `[sql_account]`, `[sql_common]` |

Each SQL sub-table has the same five keys: `host`, `user`, `password`, `database`, `port`.
This removes the legacy trap recorded in the old `parse_sql_config` / `parse_db_sql_config`
pair, where the same key name meant different field orders on the two sides
(`<host> <user> <password> <database> [port]` on the game server versus
`<host> <database> <user> <password> <port>` on the DB server).

### 169.3 Strictness: three distinct failure classes

`ConfigError` separates the cases so an operator learns what went wrong:

| variant | meaning | example |
|---|---|---|
| `Read` | the file could not be read | wrong path, permissions |
| `Syntax` | not well-formed TOML | `mother_port = `, `[unclosed` |
| `Value` | parsed, but a key is wrong | `mother_port = "not a port"`, unknown key |

The split is made by parsing into a `toml::Table` first and only then calling `try_into`, so the
distinction does not depend on `toml::de::ErrorKind` (which is not public in `toml` 0.8).

Two deliberate strictness choices, both pinned by tests:

- **An unknown key is an error.** `#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]` on all three structs. A
  misspelled setting fails at startup instead of silently keeping its default. This reverses the
  old behaviour, which ignored unknown keys; the deleted test
  `test_game_config_unknown_keys_ignored` recorded the old leniency.
- **Booleans must be TOML booleans.** The legacy parser accepted `1`, `true`, and `t` for a
  boolean. `test_server = 1` is now a `Value` error. A legacy file is therefore not silently
  half-readable.

### 169.4 The `SqlConfig` to connection-URL conversion

`SqlConfig::connection_url()` returns `mysql://user:password@host:port/database`. A zero `port`
omits the authority port so the client library uses its default. The user and password are
**percent-encoded** (RFC 3986 unreserved set), because an unencoded `@` or `/` in a password
would redirect the connection to a different host. `SqlConfig::is_configured()` requires both a
host and a database, so an unset connection is detectable before any SQL is attempted.

No binary constructs a pool from this URL yet. The pool in `db/src/pool.rs` is still never
constructed by either binary (see `docs/STATUS.md`, "What the binaries actually do"), so the
conversion is available but unconsumed. It exists because M1 names it and M2 needs it.

One caveat found while testing, recorded because it is a real trap: a **single** legacy scalar
line such as `mother_port=50080` is also valid TOML, because TOML permits `key=value` without
surrounding spaces. Such a line is accepted. A whole legacy `CONFIG` is not accepted, because its
space-separated list and SQL lines are not TOML values. The test
`a_realistic_legacy_config_file_is_rejected` pins the realistic case, and
`a_legacy_sql_line_cannot_silently_become_a_toml_string` pins that the old one-line SQL value
cannot be mis-read as a `player_sql` string.

Two container limits shaped the verification and are worth recording:

- `ss` and `netstat` produce no output in this container, so a "is it listening" check that relies

  Python instead.
- `db-server` writes no INFO output unless `RUST_LOG` is set, because its `--verbose` path calls
  `init_from_env()`. This is pre-existing behaviour and is not changed here. Piping a long-running
  server through `head` also truncates the log; the run was repeated writing to a file.

## 170. The DB peer answers BOOT: lazy pool, fail-closed peer trust, and the empty boot payload (M2)

This is the first slice of milestone M2 (see `docs/STATUS.md`). Section 169 built the TOML
configuration for both binaries and left the database half of M1 open. This section does not touch
that open item. It makes `db-server` do one real thing over a real socket: accept a peer, classify
it, authorize it through the fail-closed policy, and answer a `BOOT` request with a legacy-shaped
boot payload.

Every behavior below was derived from the legacy source and, where the legacy behavior was subtle
or surprising, independently re-verified against the checked-in tree. The verification is recorded
in 170.7.

### 170.1 What changed

| File | Change |
| --- | --- |
| `db/src/pool.rs` | new `ConnectionPool::lazy`, which performs no network I/O |
| `db-server/src/peer_auth.rs` | **new**. Classifies a connection's transport identity into a role |
| `db-server/src/peer_policy.rs` | `AuthorizationEffect::None`; BOOT allowed for authenticated peers |
| `db-server/src/item_id_range.rs` | **new**. The item-ID range FIFO and its zero fallback |
| `db-server/src/boot_empty.rs` | **new**. Composes and encodes an empty-table boot response |
| `db-server/src/main.rs` | binds the service, admits and authorizes peers, answers BOOT |
| `db-server/tests/boot_process.rs` | **new**. Two process-level tests over real TCP |
| `common/src/config.rs` | `trusted_game_peers` and `trusted_auth_peers` |
| `common/tests/config_test.rs` | a `trusted_peers` module and full-document coverage |
| `config/db.toml.example` | documents the trust lists and the lazy pools |

### 170.2 The SQL pool is lazy, and that is a deliberate difference from the legacy

The legacy DB server connects to its database during startup and refuses to serve without it. This
server must start without a reachable database, because the acceptance test for this section is
"spawn the binary, send BOOT, parse the reply", and the agent container has no MySQL or MariaDB
(169.9).

`ConnectionPool::lazy` is the seam. It applies the same `max_connections`, `min_connections`,
`acquire_timeout`, `idle_timeout`, and `max_lifetime` settings as `ConnectionPool::new`, and it
parses the URL, so a malformed URL is still reported at startup. It uses `connect_lazy`, so **no
TCP connection is attempted until a query runs**. The first query still fails if nothing is
listening on the database port, and it fails then, not at startup.

This is not a readiness signal and the code says so. A pool that cannot even be built is logged and
left absent rather than being fatal, because boot is answered from in-memory sections.

A first attempt used `ConnectionPool::with_retry` with one retry and a zero delay, on the theory
that a refused connection would fail fast. That was wrong: the process hung before the listener came
up, and the test timed out at the readiness probe with no log line past configuration. Port 1 is
closed on loopback, so a connect should be refused immediately, but the retry-and-connect path did
not return within the readiness window. The lesson is that "lazy" has to mean *no connection
attempt*, not "a connection attempt that is expected to fail quickly". `connect_lazy` is the only
construct that actually guarantees the property, and the test now proves the listener comes up with
a deliberately unreachable database.

### 170.3 Peer trust is transport identity, and it defaults to denying everyone

The legacy DB protocol has no peer-authentication exchange. The only related controls are an
optional source-address filter on the listener and a raw `bAuthServer` byte inside the setup
request. Neither is a credential. `AGENTS.md` already states that a source filter is not role
authentication.

`db-server::peer_auth` therefore names what it actually does: it compares a connection's
`SocketAddr` against two operator-supplied allowlists and returns a `DbPeerRole`. It is not
authentication, it is not a substitute for a credential-based adapter, and the module documentation
says so in those words.

Three behaviors are deliberate:

- **Both lists default to empty, which refuses every connection.** With no entry, the peer stays
  `Unclassified`, its `DbPeerPolicy` stays unauthenticated, every operation is denied including the
  read-only boot request, and the connection is closed without a reply. A server that serves nobody
  is safe but useless, so the binary logs a warning at startup that names the missing setting.
- **The source port is ignored, the host is not.** A long-lived peer's source port is chosen by the
  operating system, so matching it would be meaningless. A configured entry may be a bare address or
  a `host:port` pair; only the host is kept.
- **One address may not hold both roles, and an unparseable entry fails startup.** A conflicting
  entry is an error rather than a silent precedence rule, so an operator cannot enable the auth role
  by accident.

When the lists are non-empty the binary logs a warning at startup that names the counts and states
that this is not authentication.

### 170.4 BOOT is authorized through the policy, and its authorization has no effect

`DbPeerOperation::Boot` already existed. Two things were added:

- `AuthorizationEffect::None`, for an authorization that is genuinely effect-free. This is a real
  state, not a placeholder: a read-only boot request must leave shared state alone, and an explicit
  variant says that rather than leaving the reader to infer it from the absence of a bind.
- The boot matrix entry: an authenticated `Game` or `Auth` peer may request BOOT, and the result is
  `AuthorizationEffect::None`. The auth slot is **not** bound by a boot request. An unauthenticated,
  revoked, or closed peer is still denied.

`AuthPeerSlotError::NoEffectToApply` was added so that an attempt to apply a non-binding effect
fails loudly instead of being ignored.

The ordering in `serve_request` is the security-relevant part. The decision is taken first; the
response is written second; the effect is applied third. So a denied request never claims the slot,
and a request whose response failed to write never claims it either.

### 170.5 The empty boot response and its exact length

`db-server/src/boot_empty.rs` composes a boot payload from a `BootFeatureProfile` and a
caller-supplied tail, with no SQL and no table loader. The active profile is the one the checked-in
legacy build compiles: `ENABLE_RENEWAL_SHOPEX`, `__EVENT_MANAGER__`, and
`__PREMIUM_PRIVATE_SHOP__` are all defined, so the active profile has **14** table sections, not 13.
The minimal profile has 11.

Every section declares its verified record width even when it carries zero rows, because the legacy
always writes the size `WORD` (170.7). The widths are asserted against the protocol's own constants
rather than literals, so a later corrected C++ width cannot leave a test asserting a stale value.

An active-profile empty boot payload is exactly **415 bytes**:

| Part | Bytes |
| --- | --- |
| declared payload length | 4 |
| version byte (`6`) | 1 |
| 14 table sections, 4 bytes each | 56 |
| x86 `time_t` | 4 |
| item-ID range header plus two records | 28 |
| GM host header | 4 |
| admin header | 4 |
| monarch header plus one 304-byte record | 308 |
| candidacy header | 4 |
| `0xffff` terminator | 2 |
| **total** | **415** |

The monarch record is emitted with a declared count of 1 even though it is all zeros, because the
legacy `CMonarch` constructor memsets the record and `LoadMonarch` returns false without writing to
it when there are no rows.

### 170.6 The item-ID range pool

`db-server/src/item_id_range.rs` models `CItemIDRangeManager` as a FIFO with a zero fallback.
`take_boot_pair` pops two ranges, which is what a single boot request consumes. The pool starts
empty, so an unconfigured server emits two zero records under the legacy count-1 header, which is
the legacy's own empty-list behavior.

Two legacy details are deliberately **not** reproduced, and both are documented in the code:

- The legacy all-zero return is specific to an *empty* list. When the list was non-empty but every
  candidate collided with a peer, the legacy falls out of its loop still holding the last popped,
  colliding range and returns *that*. Reproducing it would mean handing a peer a range another peer
  already holds.
- The legacy logs ten `sys_err` lines before giving up. Logging belongs to the caller, so the pool
  exposes a collision counter instead.

The pop happens before the collision test in the legacy too, so one call can consume several list
entries. `next_range` documents that, and points an adapter that needs collision rejection at
`next_unchecked` plus `record_collision` plus retry.

### 170.7 Independent verification of the legacy `QUERY_BOOT`

A read-only worker re-derived the legacy behavior from the checked-in tree and returned
`CONFIRMED` on all four claims, with one correction. All line numbers are from
`server/server/db/`.

**Claim 1, CONFIRMED.** `CClientManager::QUERY_BOOT` (`ClientManager.cpp:436`) calls
`CItemIDRangeManager::GetRange()` exactly twice, at `ClientManager.cpp:588-589`.
`GetRange` (`ItemIDRangeManager.cpp:60-85`) pops the front *before* the peer-collision test, and its
only value-returning path is reachable only after a `pop_front`, so every successful call removes at
least one element. Two consecutive calls therefore return two successive, distinct ranges. The
worker also confirmed that `GetRange` has exactly one other caller, `CPeer::SendSpareItemIDRange`
(`Peer.cpp:146`), which is a different function.

**Claim 2, CONFIRMED.** `ItemIDRangeManager.cpp:62-65` zeroes all three fields before consulting the
list, and the fall-through loop at lines 81-84 only logs, so an empty list yields the all-zero record.
The worker added a precision this section adopts: the ten-line loop also runs when the list was
non-empty but every candidate collided, and the return value is then the last colliding range, not
the zeros.

**Claim 3, CONFIRMED.** `ClientManager.cpp:591-594` writes `sizeof(TItemIDRangeTable)`, the literal
count `1`, and then **two** records. The worker confirmed from the game side
(`server/server/game/input_db.cpp:776-791`) that the reader consumes `size` records and then `size`
records again with no check on the count word. A rewrite that trusted the count as a total would
desynchronize here. The count word is a per-half stride, not a total.

**Claim 4, CONFIRMED.** `ClientManager.cpp:620-622` writes `sizeof(TMonarchInfo)`, the literal count
`1`, and the single record from `CMonarch::instance().GetMonarch()`. `Monarch.cpp:8-11` memsets the
member in the constructor, and `LoadMonarch` (`Monarch.cpp:175-206`) returns false at line 185-186
on zero rows without writing to it, so a never-loaded monarch is one all-zero record with a declared
count of 1. The worker noted that the `memset` spells the type `MonarchInfo` (the `typedef` alias)
while the `Encode` call spells it `TMonarchInfo` (the struct tag); `tables.h:1574-1579` shows they
are the same type, and the probe measured both at 304 bytes.

**Correction to my own count: the active profile has 14 sections, not 13.** The worker cross-checked
two ways: fourteen `sizeof(WORD) + sizeof(WORD)` record pairs in the size formula at
`ClientManager.cpp:451-470`, and 28 `EncodeWORD` calls across lines 506-582. The likeliest source of
a 13-count is section 8, which reuses `sizeof(TItemAttrTable)` and so looks like a repeat of
section 7. My implementation already had 14 from the `ACTIVE_SECTION_KINDS` list, so no code changed;
the number in this section is the verified one.

**Widths, measured rather than hand-summed.** `server/server/common/tables.h` is inside
`#pragma pack(1)` (line 345 to line 2291), so all three structs are packed. The worker compiled the
verbatim struct bodies with `i686-linux-gnu-g++-12 -static` and read `__builtin_offsetof`:

| Struct | Size | Field offsets |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `TItemIDRangeTable` | 12 | `dwMin` 0, `dwMax` 4, `dwUsableItemIDMin` 8 |
| `TMonarchInfo` | 304 | `pid` 0, `money` 16, `name` 48, `date` 176 |
| `MonarchCandidacy` | 68 | `pid` 0, `name` 4, `date` 36 |

`sizeof(time_t)` is 4 on i686, which is the bare `time_t` at `ClientManager.cpp:585-586`. The probe
re-measured its controls in the same run: packed two-`long` 8, packed `BYTE`/`WORD`/`DWORD` 7, packed
three-`DWORD` 12, `sizeof(long)` 4, `sizeof(unsigned int)` 4, `sizeof(int64_t)` 8. All three target
structs are 4-, 8-, and 1-byte fields in a packed struct, so they are identical on a 64-bit host;
the probe is i686 anyway, and the controls would have caught a 64-bit read.

**One legacy defect is not reproduced.** Sections 1, 2, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10, and 11 take `&vec[0]`
unconditionally in the legacy, which is undefined behavior on an empty vector, then do a zero-length
encode. This implementation iterates, so an empty section is well defined.

**Counts are narrowed to 16 bits on the wire.** `EncodeWORD` takes a `WORD`
(`PeerBase.h:37`), so every `size_t` and every `int` count is truncated to 16 bits by the legacy.
`empty_sections` returns `EmptyBootError::RecordWidthOverflow` rather than truncating silently.

### 170.8 Runtime evidence

A real `db-server` process was started on `127.0.0.1:39188` with only
`trusted_game_peers = ["127.0.0.1"]` set and no SQL configuration at all. A raw socket client wrote
the exact legacy boot frame: header `9`, handle `0x1234`, a 24-byte little-endian length, and the
24-byte `TPacketGDBoot` payload.

The reply:

| Field | Observed |
| --- | --- |
| header | `43` (`HEADER_DG_BOOT`) |
| handle | `0` (the legacy zero handle for the unsolicited boot reply) |
| declared length | `415` |
| bytes actually read | `415` |
| first four bytes | `9f 01 00 00`, which is 415 little-endian |
| version byte | `6` |
| `time_t` | `1790404713`, a real clock value, not a constant |
| last two bytes | `ff ff`, the `0xffff` terminator |

The server log for that exchange:

```
WARN  trusted peer addresses are configured. This is transport identity, NOT authentication: ...
INFO  New game server connection addr=127.0.0.1:58692 peer_id=1
INFO  DB peer transport identity classified addr=127.0.0.1:58692 role=Game
INFO  answered BOOT with an empty-table boot payload addr=127.0.0.1:58692 request_kind="boot"
      handle=4660 payload_len=415
INFO  DB peer closed cleanly addr=127.0.0.1:58692
```

The same run shows the two startup warnings the design calls for: the non-authentication warning for
a configured list, and, when the list is empty, the warning that every connection will be refused.

The reply was additionally decoded by `protocol::db_boot` in `db-server/tests/boot_process.rs`, not
by arithmetic in the test, and asserted to have 14 empty sections, a real clock, the count-1 range
header, and the `0xffff` terminator.

### 170.9 The two process-level tests

`db-server/tests/boot_process.rs` starts the built binary twice.

- `a_trusted_peer_receives_a_parseable_empty_boot_payload` starts the server with the loopback
  address trusted, connects, writes the exact 24-byte boot payload in the legacy envelope, reads one
  frame, and decodes it with `parse_db_boot_frame_bytes`.
- `an_unlisted_peer_is_closed_without_a_reply` starts the server with the trust list removed, and
  asserts that the peer receives nothing. This is what makes the fail-closed default a socket
  behavior rather than only a policy value.

Both tests bind an ephemeral loopback port, write a temporary `db.toml` whose SQL points at the
closed port 1, and run the child in a temporary directory. The second test is the regression test for
170.2: the listener must come up with an unreachable database.

### 170.10 What this section does not do

- **No table loading.** All 14 sections are empty, and the code says so on the wire. The server has
  not read a single `mob`, `item`, `shop`, `skill`, `refine`, `item_attr`, `item_rare`, `banword`,
  `land`, `object_proto`, `object`, `event`, `market_price`, or `renewal_shop` row.
- **No item-ID ranges are ever allocated.** The pool is empty, so every boot reply carries two zero
  ranges. Nothing in this section builds ranges from the database.
- **No monarch or GM-host data.** The monarch record is the constructor's zeros, and the GM host and
  admin lists are empty. Loading them needs a table loader and a cache.
- **No response for any other request.** Setup, horse-name, channel lookup, login-by-key, player
  load, add-affect, and remove-affect are authorized through the policy and then logged as
  unimplemented. None is acknowledged and none is answered.
- **No credential-based peer authentication.** 170.3 is transport identity only. A real deployment
  needs a credential exchange the legacy protocol does not have.
- **M1's database half is still open.** The DDL, the seed, and the `DATABASE_URL`-gated test are
  still unwritten, and the container still has no reachable MariaDB.

### 170.11 A SIGTERM race in the game server, found by the new gate load

The first full-workspace run of this section failed one test that had passed in every earlier run:
`game_server_process_starts_and_shuts_down_cleanly_on_sigterm`, at the assertion
`output.status.success()`. It passed in isolation and passed on the next five consecutive runs, so it
was a race, and it reproduced under the heavier load of a full workspace test run.

The cause was an ordering bug in `game-server/src/main.rs`, not in the test. `wait_for_shutdown_signal`
was an `async fn` that installed the SIGTERM handler only when it was first polled, and it was first
polled inside `run_accept_loop`. The order in `main` was:

1. bind the TCP listener,
2. spawn the game loop,
3. call `run_accept_loop`, which creates the signal stream and starts polling it.

The kernel keeps the default SIGTERM disposition until step 3. A test, a supervisor, or a real
deployment that sees the port open at step 1 and sends SIGTERM in the window before step 3 gets the
default action: the process dies on the signal instead of shutting down, and the exit status is
signal-terminated rather than successful. This is a real deployment hazard, not only a test artifact:
any orchestrator that restarts on SIGTERM would see a hard kill rather than a clean stop.

The fix splits the old function into two:

- `arm_shutdown_signal()` is **synchronous** and creates the signal streams, which is the call that
  installs the handlers. It runs before `setup_tcp_listener`, so "the port is open" now implies "SIGTERM
  is handled".
- `ShutdownSignal::wait()` is the async half that awaits delivery.

SIGINT is now registered the same way, through `signal::unix::signal(SignalKind::interrupt())`, rather
than through `ctrl_c()`. `ctrl_c()` also installs lazily on first poll, so leaving it in place would
have left the identical window on SIGINT.

`run_accept_loop` takes the already-armed `ShutdownSignal` and pins the wait future **once** with
`Box::pin`. Recreating the future on each `select!` iteration would drop the signal streams every
pass and lose a signal that arrived between two accepts.

A handler-registration failure is now fatal instead of being reported later, because a process that
cannot handle SIGTERM cannot shut down cleanly.

## 171. M3 part 1: `DbRequestService` in the live binary, and the SETUP reply

Section 170 made the DB peer able to answer BOOT. This section binds that
service into the real `db-server` process and adds the second live answer the
vertical slice needs: the SETUP reply (`HEADER_DG_MAP_LOCATIONS`). Section 170
is not edited.

### 171.1 `db-server/src/main.rs` had to be rebuilt first

`db-server/src/main.rs` is an untracked file in this worktree, so Git could
not restore it, and the last edit left it truncated to 423 lines with an
unclosed `impl DbService {` block. No backup on disk was current: every
`/tmp` copy was a 495-line pre-Section-169 revision. `target/debug/db-server`
was a compiled Section 170 binary, which is a receipt and not a source.

The file was reconstructed from the two things that were still authoritative,
the Section 169 configuration work and the Section 170 service seam, then
installed and compiled. The first build surfaced five real mismatches, all of
the "this name lives in the other module" kind:

| Symptom | Real location |
| --- | --- |
| `DbServiceOutcome` unresolved | `db_server::service`, not `db_server::session` |
| `DbPeerRole` unresolved | added to the `peer_policy` import |
| `DbService.requests` type wrong | the installed responder is the fourth generic, so `DbRequestService<UnavailableHorseNames, (), LiveBootResponder, EchoSetupResponder>` |
| `LiveBootResponder` not `Debug` | `DbRequestService` derives `Debug`, so the seam type must too |
| boot state declared twice | `main.rs` still held the Section 170 fields that `LiveBootResponder` now owns |

`BootResponseError` also gained a `Compose` variant, because the live
composer needs to report a composition failure rather than encoding a short
frame.

### 171.2 BOOT is now composed per request, not replayed from a snapshot

`BootResponseAdapter` is an immutable snapshot, which is the right shape for a
test and the wrong shape for a live server: legacy `QUERY_BOOT` calls
`CItemIDRangeManager::GetRange()` twice per request, so each answer must
consume two successive ranges from the persistent FIFO. A snapshot replayed
the same two ranges to every peer and would hand out colliding item IDs.

The fix is a seam, not a bigger adapter:

- `protocol`-level encoding is unchanged, and still the single source of the
  active 415-byte empty payload.
- `BootResponder` has one method, `respond() -> Result<DbFrame, BootResponseError>`.
- `impl BootResponder for ()` returns `BootResponseError::Unavailable`. It is
  fail-closed and is only ever selected when explicitly wrapped in `Some`.
- `impl<T> BootResponder for Arc<T>` forwards, so the live responder can be
  shared by every connection task without cloning boot state.
- `DbRequestService` prefers the per-request responder and falls back to the
  immutable adapter when none is installed, so the pre-Section-171 tests that
  rely on the snapshot keep exercising that path.

`LiveBootResponder` in `main.rs` owns the item-range pool, the clock, and the
injected time source. The accept loop hands every connection an
`Arc<DbService>`, so all peers share one pool and ranges stay globally unique.

### 171.3 Two setup request shapes exist and only one of them is answered

The source audit that preceded this section established the frame contract
(`ClientManager.cpp:1284`, `QUERY_SETUP`):

- A setup request with `bAuthServer != 0` gets **no bytes at all**. The legacy
  auth branch returns before it builds a buffer.
- An ordinary game setup request gets exactly one frame: header
  `HEADER_DG_MAP_LOCATIONS = 0xfe`, handle `0`, payload `BYTE count` followed
  by `count` records of 146 bytes. The count is always at least 1, because the
  requesting peer's own location is appended last.
- No incoming setup handle is echoed. There is no setup version byte and no
  per-table count word.

`SetupReplyOutcome` therefore has two variants, and the distinction is load
bearing. `Silent` means "write nothing", not "write an empty frame". A
zero-length `0xfe` frame would make the peer read a count byte that does not
exist, so the service reports `DbServiceOutcome::NoResponse` for the auth path
and the connection waits for the next request. Reporting `Responded` there
would have claimed a frame that does not exist.

The `bAuthServer` byte is read only to choose the silent branch. It is raw
payload, never a credential. The role decision belongs to `DbPeerPolicy`, and
it is already made before the service is reached.

### 171.4 Authorization: an ordinary game setup is a new permitted operation

Section 170 gave BOOT an explicit `AuthorizationEffect::None` so an
authenticated peer could request it without binding the auth slot. Ordinary
game setup needs the same treatment, because it is a normal game-role
operation that the legacy server answers for any connected game peer.

`DbPeerOperation::GameSetup` is authorized for authenticated Game and Auth
peers with `AuthorizationEffect::None`. Two properties were kept deliberately:

- The **auth-mode** request path is still restricted to the Auth role. A
  `bAuthServer != 0` request from an ordinary game peer is rejected before
  the service is reached, so it can never be answered with silence by
  accident, and it can never bind the auth slot through the game path.
- The setup reply **discloses** a peer's public IP, listen port, and map list.
  That is why the unlisted-peer test is a required case rather than a
  nicety: authorization has to run before a single byte is composed.

Decoder tests confirm that an auth-mode request carrying login records is
rejected by the decoder, before any policy dispatch, so `bAuthServer` cannot be
used to smuggle a login path through the setup arm.

### 171.5 `protocol/src/db_map_locations.rs`

New transport-free module, registered in `protocol/src/lib.rs`:

- `HEADER_DG_MAP_LOCATIONS = 0xfe` and `HEADER_DG_P2P = 0xff`. Both are
  declared here rather than in `setup.rs` so the reply direction owns its own
  names. `0xff` is still the same numeric value as `HEADER_GD_SETUP`; the two
  belong to opposite directions and must not be merged.
- `MapLocation` is exactly 146 bytes: 32 signed 32-bit little-endian map
  indices at offset 0, 16 raw host bytes at offset 128, and an unsigned 16-bit
  little-endian port at offset 144.
- One record is a 147-byte payload, and the complete frame is 156 bytes:
  9-byte envelope plus 147-byte payload.
- The count is checked with `u8::try_from`, so 256 records is an error rather
  than a silent truncation to 0. Legacy truncates a `size_t` count into a
  `BYTE`; that defect is recorded, not reproduced.
- Decoding validates the count against the actual payload length, so a short
  payload is rejected instead of being over-read.
- The host field is zero-filled past the end of a short input string, so
  encoding is deterministic. Legacy leaves those bytes uninitialized.

16 codec tests cover the golden single-peer frame, the round trip, both
truncation defects, the 255-record boundary, and the 256-record rejection.

### 171.6 `db-server/src/setup_reply.rs`

`compose_setup_reply` builds the reply from the request alone. The legacy
handler copies the peer's own public IP, listen port, and map array into the
record it echoes back, so nothing is read from SQL, configuration, or another
peer. That is the whole reason this slice is small: a fresh single-peer DB
needs no state to answer, and the first honest implementation is therefore the
one-peer case.

`leading_map_count` takes the contiguous leading entries of the 32-slot map
array. The legacy list is `MAP_ALLOW` plus the channel's own entry, and a
33rd entry would overwrite `dwLoginCount` in the packed request. Capping at 32
and stopping at the first zero is the deliberate, non-overwriting choice.

13 unit tests cover the golden single-record frame, the payload shape, the
echo of the request's own fields, trimming at a zero terminator, a non-zero
slot after that terminator, all 32 slots non-zero, the silent auth branch, any
non-zero auth byte, a request that also carries login records, a high-byte
public IP kept as raw storage, an empty map list, determinism, and the decoder
still refusing a short setup payload.

The one record this produces is the peer's own location, which matches the
legacy ordering rule that the requesting peer is appended last. The
multi-peer case is not implemented: it needs a connected-peer registry, which
does not exist yet, and inventing a global would have been a guess about
authority. This is recorded as a known gap, not as a complete SETUP.

### 171.7 Service wiring

`DbRequestService` now has four generics, `DbRequestService<L, C = (), R = (), S = ()>`:

- `with_boot_responder` installs the per-request BOOT seam.
- `with_setup_responder` installs the per-request setup composer.
- `has_boot_responder` and `has_setup_responder` let a test assert which path
  is live without reaching into private state.
- Absent responders stay honest `NotReady` outcomes. No bytes are written.

**A documented claim that was false, and the fix.** `with_setup_responder`
carried a doc comment promising it "composes with `Self::with_boot_responder`
in either order". It did not. `with_boot_responder` lived on
`impl<L, C> DbRequestService<L, C, (), ()>`, so once a setup composer was
installed the boot seam was unreachable and the call did not compile. The
method now lives on `impl<L, C, S> DbRequestService<L, C, (), S>`, which covers
`S = ()` as well, and the older narrower definition was removed so the two do
not become ambiguous. Both builders still require the *other* seam to be
absent, so installing a seam twice remains a compile error rather than a silent
replacement of a live composer. A test now pins both orders.

Both accessors were also moved onto the fully generic
`impl<L, C, R, S> DbRequestService<L, C, R, S>`: on their original narrow impls
they were missing from a service that had both seams installed, which is
exactly the state a live server is in.

`DbServiceError` gained `SetupReply(SetupReplyError)`.

`DbRequestService::handle` had reached 104 lines and tripped
`clippy::too_many_lines`. The setup branch was extracted into a private
`respond_to_setup` method rather than suppressed. The extraction also let the
silent-auth decision live in one place with a doc comment explaining why it
is `NoResponse` and not `Responded`.

`EchoSetupResponder` in `main.rs` is the live implementation, and it delegates
to `compose_setup_reply`.

### 171.8 Lint findings, all fixed by refactoring

Four strict-Clippy classes came out of the new code and none were suppressed:

- `payload.push(self.records.len() as u8)` and three test casts became
  `u8::try_from` / `i32::try_from` with real error handling. Two of the
  conversions carry a `MAP_LOCATION_HOST_BYTES` bound, which makes the "32
  slots fit a signed 32-bit field" reasoning local instead of assumed.
- `assert_eq!(x.eq(&Variant::Silent), false)` was a literal-bool comparison
  that also duplicated the call; it became a `matches!` assertion.
- `(slot as i32) + 1` in a test became an iterator over the expected indices.
- A rustdoc link to `[HEADER_DG_BOOT]` failed under
  `RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings"` because the constant is not in scope in that
  module. The link became a plain code span, since the surrounding comment
  already names the header.

The first compile of the new tests had two test-side defects worth recording.
`start_server` returns `(ProcessGuard, SocketAddr)` and is not fallible, so
`start_server().expect(...)` did not compile, and `&[0_i32; 32 - maps.len()]`
is not a const expression. Both are test bugs, not product bugs, and the fix
was to use the existing `start_server(binary, trusted)` helper and to compare
against a sub-slice of a fixed array.

Three service-level tests were added next, and all three earned their place:

- `the_installed_seams_report_presence_in_either_order` found the real API
  defect recorded in 171.7.
- `an_installed_setup_composer_writes_one_frame_and_reports_its_own_handle`
  pins the `Responded` outcome, the zero handle, and the
  `1 + 146`-byte payload. Its fixture first pushed `0xfe` into the *payload*
  and then asserted the payload started with the count byte, which failed at
  `254 != 1`. The frame header and the payload are different fields, and the
  fixture had conflated them.
- `a_silent_setup_composer_reports_no_response_and_writes_nothing` pins the
  auth-branch outcome at the dispatch level, so the silent path is verified
  here and end to end rather than at only one of the two levels.
